weekly.title: The Resurrection
weekly.line: Every Sunday is a little Easter: the day Christ rose from the dead.

psalm.text: This is the day that the Lord has made. We will rejoice and be glad in it!

reading.text: Why do you seek the living among the dead? He isn't here, but is risen.

midday.text: I am the resurrection and the life.

evening.text: You will show me the path of life. In your presence is fullness of joy.

weekly.intention: Where could you bring new life today: a fresh start, a reconciliation, a word of encouragement?
weekly.ideaLine: Every week can start again. What deserves a fresh start in your life?
weekly.look: Look how low Cuyp sets the horizon: the river and its ships take up a thin strip, and almost everything else is sky. The clouds are lit gold along their tops, as if the light has just arrived. The ships are gathered and waiting, sails ready, with nowhere yet to be. That is what a Sunday can be: a wide, open space above the busy waterline of our lives, and a moment to set out again. Christians keep Sunday because they believe the light came back on the first day of the week, and it can come back to us too.
weekly.psalmNote: Psalm 118 was sung by pilgrims climbing to the Temple in Jerusalem, a song of thanks from people who had been close to defeat and were rescued. “This is the day” was not about a pleasant morning. It meant: this, the day God turned things round. Every Sunday Christians borrow the line for Easter, and offer it to any of us who need a new start.
weekly.prayer: God of the first day, you made this morning and handed it to me unused. Whatever went wrong last week, let it stay there. Show me one thing that deserves a fresh start, and give me the nerve to begin it before tonight. Let me be glad in the day you have made. Amen.

weekly.title: The Angels and the Unseen
weekly.line: The week begins by remembering that we live among more than we can see.

psalm.text: Praise the Lord, all you his angels, who are mighty in strength, who fulfil his word.

reading.text: Don't forget to show hospitality to strangers, for in doing so, some have entertained angels without knowing it.

midday.text: He will put his angels in charge of you, to guard you in all your ways.

evening.text: The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them.

weekly.intention: Who is the stranger you could welcome today?
weekly.ideaLine: There is more to the world, and to people, than we can see or measure.
weekly.look: Bierstadt gives us a dirt road, a grove of trees, a quiet lake, and then mountains so tall they fade into haze. Your eye keeps travelling further than you expected. That is the feeling he was after: the near things are clear, but the far things are vast and only half seen. Christians say the world is like that. Behind the ordinary road you walk each day lies more than you can measure, and the same is true of the people you pass on it.
weekly.psalmNote: This line closes a psalm of thanks. Having praised God for forgiveness and mercy, the singer runs out of room and calls on the angels, the unseen servants of God, to join in. For the first people who prayed it, the world was full of more than they could see. Today’s idea begins there.
weekly.prayer: Lord of all that is seen and unseen, you are praised by voices I will never hear. Open my eyes today to more than the surface of things. When I meet a stranger, let me remember there is more to them than I can see, and let me treat them gently. Amen.

weekly.title: Turning Around
weekly.line: Tuesday remembers John the Baptist, who called people to turn around and start again.

psalm.text: Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.

reading.text: Make ready the way of the Lord! Make his paths straight!

midday.text: In returning and rest you will be saved. In quietness and in confidence will be your strength.

evening.text: As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us.

weekly.intention: What habit or attitude do you want to turn away from, starting today?
weekly.ideaLine: It's never too late to turn around. What would you like to leave behind?
weekly.look: The young man grips the tiller and steers for a shining castle in the clouds, leaving his guardian angel behind on the bank. Look at the river, though: it does not run towards the castle at all, but slips away past the rocks towards something he cannot yet see. Cole is gently honest about youth, which is sure of its course and often wrong. Starting again usually begins with noticing that the river and the dream have parted, and choosing to turn the boat.
weekly.psalmNote: Tradition links this psalm to King David after he had taken another man’s wife and arranged that man’s death, so it is the prayer of someone with no excuses left. Notice that he does not ask to be patched up; he asks for a new heart. Starting again, in the Bible, is less about trying harder and more about being made new.
weekly.prayer: God of second chances, I cannot scrub my own heart clean, so I ask you to do it. Show me what I am carrying that I should put down, and give me the courage to turn round today, not someday. Make the way in front of me straight. Amen.

weekly.title: Keeping Faith
weekly.line: By tradition Judas agreed to betray Jesus on a Wednesday. Today we pray to be faithful.

psalm.text: His compassion doesn't fail. It is new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.

reading.text: He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.

midday.text: Where you go, I will go; and where you stay, I will stay.

evening.text: Your loving kindness, Lord, is in the heavens. Your faithfulness reaches to the skies.

weekly.intention: Who is relying on you? Keep one promise to them today, however small.
weekly.ideaLine: Trust is built in small promises kept. Who is relying on you?
weekly.look: Rembrandt painted himself again and again, and here he is at fifty-three, a few years after going bankrupt. Look at the furrowed brow and the deep-set grey eyes that meet yours. He does not flatter himself or hide the wear. A face like this is built slowly, by thousands of small choices, and so is trust. Nobody becomes reliable in one grand gesture. It happens in the promise to ring back, the lift you said you’d give, the thing you said you’d do and did.
weekly.psalmNote: These words come from Lamentations, a set of poems written among the ruins of Jerusalem after the city fell. The writer has lost almost everything, yet notices that God’s kindness turns up again each morning, like dawn. Faithfulness here is not a feeling but a habit of showing up, which is exactly what keeping your word asks of us.
weekly.prayer: God, you have never once failed to bring the morning. Make me the kind of person others can lean on. Help me remember the small things I have promised, and keep them without fuss, so that someone today finds me faithful in very little. Amen.

weekly.title: Friends at the Table
weekly.line: On a Thursday Jesus shared bread with his friends and washed their feet.

psalm.text: See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!

reading.text: No longer do I call you servants. I have called you friends.

midday.text: Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.

evening.text: You prepare a table before me. My cup runs over.

weekly.intention: Who could you share a meal or a real conversation with this week?
weekly.ideaLine: A shared table and a real conversation are among life's deepest goods.
weekly.look: Rembrandt paints an old story from the Roman poet Ovid: Philemon and Baucis, a poor elderly couple, take in two strangers that richer neighbours had turned away, and share what little they have. The guests turn out to be the gods Jupiter and Mercury. Notice how small and plain the room is, and how the golden light gathers around the table itself. Rembrandt suggests that the holy is found where someone pulls up a chair for a stranger. Christians hear an echo of Jesus at supper, calling those around his table not servants but friends.
weekly.psalmNote: Psalm 133 is one of the short “songs of ascent” sung by families travelling together to Jerusalem for the great feasts. Cousins, neighbours and old rivals walked the same road and ate together on the way. The psalm calls that togetherness good and pleasant, a gift to be enjoyed and not merely a duty. Friendship, it suggests, is one of the ways God blesses us.
weekly.prayer: Lord Jesus, you called your followers friends, and you ate and talked with them as equals. Thank you for the people who have sat at my table and stayed. Make me a better friend today: slower to talk about myself, quicker to listen, and glad to share what I have. Amen.

weekly.title: The Cross
weekly.line: Every Friday remembers the day Jesus gave himself for the world.

psalm.text: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?

reading.text: Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.

midday.text: Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing.

evening.text: He was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities; by his wounds we are healed.

weekly.intention: Is there someone you need to forgive, even a little, today?
weekly.ideaLine: The greatest love gives itself away. Where could you give a little more?
weekly.look: Fra Angelico shows Mary seated low, as the title suggests: the Madonna of Humility, a way of painting her that comes from the Latin for earth. Behind her, two angels hold up a rich patterned cloth, the kind once hung behind a king. Yet she does not look at it. She looks down at the baby lying across her lap. Glory is there, but love is turned towards someone else. On a Friday, it is hard not to think ahead to the grown son she will one day hold again.
weekly.psalmNote: Jesus cried these words from the cross, and they were already old: they open a psalm of someone who feels utterly abandoned yet keeps praying. The psalm ends in trust and praise. That Jesus prayed it tells us self-giving love goes all the way down into the dark, and does not stop loving there.
weekly.prayer: Jesus, you prayed the words of the abandoned so that no one would pray them alone. Teach me a little of your self-giving love. Where I have been holding something back today, my time, my attention or my forgiveness, help me give it away freely, as you gave yourself for me. Amen.

weekly.title: Rest and Remembering
weekly.line: Saturday is the Sabbath, the day of rest, when Christians also remember those who have died.

psalm.text: My soul rests in God alone. My salvation is from him.

reading.text: Come to me, all you who labour and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.

midday.text: Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.

evening.text: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more.

weekly.intention: Who have you lost? Give thanks for them today, and let yourself rest.
weekly.ideaLine: Stop, rest, and remember the people who made you who you are.
weekly.look: In the story, Joseph took Mary and the baby to Egypt to escape King Herod’s soldiers, so this is a family on the run. Yet Gerard David paints not the danger but the pause: Mary sits on a rock, her blue gown spread around her, the child safe in her lap, the long hilly road stretching away behind them. The journey is not over, but for now they stop. Rest is not giving up; it is how people on a hard road keep going, carrying with them those they love.
weekly.psalmNote: This psalm was prayed by someone under pressure, surrounded by people trying to topple him. Its answer is not a plan but a stillness: I rest in God, and that is enough. For people who first prayed it, rest was not a luxury but trust, and it opens space today to stop, and remember who held us up.
weekly.prayer: Lord, my soul is restless and my days are full. Let me stop today and rest in you alone. I thank you for the people who made me who I am, especially those I have lost. Keep them in your care, and keep me in your peace. Amen.

lent.title: Lent: Into the Wilderness
lent.line: For forty days Jesus fasted in the desert. Lent is our forty days.

psalm.text: As the deer pants for the water brooks, so my soul pants after you, God.

reading.text: Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness, and he fasted forty days and forty nights.

midday.text: Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God's mouth.

evening.text: Search me, God, and know my heart. Lead me in the everlasting way.

lent.intention: What one thing will you give up or take up this week, to make room for God?
lent.ideaLine: Forty days of less: making room for what matters most.
lent.look: Bellini puts Saint Jerome at the mouth of a rough cave, almost bare, sitting on a rock with a book open. Jerome went into the desert near Bethlehem and spent years translating the Bible into Latin. Notice how calm he is: the wilderness has not emptied him, it has cleared space for the one thing he is reading. Behind him the landscape opens wide. Lent works like this. Giving something up is not the point; the point is the room it leaves.
lent.psalmNote: This psalm was prayed by someone far from the Temple in Jerusalem, perhaps in exile, who missed God the way a thirsty animal misses water. Thirst is the right word for Lent. When we go without something for forty days, we start to notice what we are really hungry for, and the psalm says that hunger, underneath the others, is for God.
lent.prayer: God, I am thirsty in ways I don’t always admit. As I begin these forty days, help me put down one thing that crowds you out, and pick up one thing that makes room. Lead me into the quiet places, and meet me there like water. Amen.

lent.title: Lent: Prayer
lent.line: The first of the three Lenten disciplines: prayer.

psalm.text: Let my prayer be set before you like incense.

reading.text: When you pray, enter into your inner room, and having shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret.

midday.text: Be still, and know that I am God.

evening.text: I will lie down in peace and sleep, for you alone, Lord, make me live in safety.

lent.intention: Before you start work or open your messages, sit for five minutes in a quiet room with the door shut, and tell God plainly what is on your mind.
lent.ideaLine: In a noisy world, stillness is where we hear what matters.
lent.look: Saenredam spent his life painting church interiors, and he made them almost empty: whitewashed walls, tall clear windows, a few small figures, if any. We stand low down by the left wall and look along it into the bright, curved apse at the far end, where a painting hangs above the altar. Nothing in the picture is hurrying. The space itself seems to listen. Silence, in the Christian sense, is not just the absence of noise but a room like this, cleared and light, where God can be heard and we can finally hear ourselves.
lent.psalmNote: Psalm 141 is an evening prayer from someone under pressure, surrounded by people who would drag them into wrongdoing. In the Temple, incense was burned every morning and evening, its smoke rising quietly. The psalmist asks that their prayer might rise the same way. It is a picture of prayer as something simple and steady, offered in stillness, without needing many words.
lent.prayer: God who hears in secret, I come to you with the noise of the day already starting. Let my prayer rise to you quietly, like incense. Teach me to shut the door for a while, inside and out, and to trust that you are there in the stillness, even when I hear nothing. Amen.

lent.title: Lent: Fasting and Simplicity
lent.line: The second discipline: fasting, which makes space for what matters.

psalm.text: Create in me a clean heart, O God.

reading.text: Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God's mouth.

midday.text: Isn't this the fast that I have chosen: to release the bonds of wickedness, and to let the oppressed go free?

evening.text: My soul thirsts for God, for the living God.

lent.intention: What could you go without today, and give the time or money to someone else?
lent.ideaLine: Going without something reminds you what you really need.
lent.look: A woman bends over her sewing, wholly absorbed, in a painting Velázquez never finished. Parts of it are still only roughly laid in, yet it hardly matters: everything you need is there, the bowed head, the light on her shoulders, the quiet work in her hands. Nothing is added for show. That is the gift of going without. When you strip something back, you notice what was holding it together all along. Fasting, in the Christian sense, is making that kind of space on purpose.
lent.psalmNote: King David is said to have prayed this psalm after his great wrong against Bathsheba and Uriah. He does not ask for a little tidying up; he asks God to create something new in him. Lent’s fasting serves the same hope: clearing away the clutter so a cleaner, simpler heart has room to grow.
lent.prayer: God who makes all things new, I come to you carrying more than I need. Create in me a clean heart. Show me one thing I can do without today, and let the space it leaves be filled with you, and with care for someone who has less than I do. Amen.

lent.title: Lent: Generosity
lent.line: The third discipline: giving to those in need, quietly.

psalm.text: Blessed is he who considers the poor.

reading.text: When you do merciful deeds, don't let your left hand know what your right hand does.

midday.text: God loves a cheerful giver.

evening.text: Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good; for his loving kindness endures forever.

lent.intention: Give something away today without telling anyone.
lent.look: Martin was a young Roman soldier who, the story goes, met a nearly naked beggar one winter’s day at the gate of Amiens in France, drew his sword, cut his own cloak in two and gave him half. El Greco fills the canvas with that moment: the great white horse, the soldier leaning down, the green cloth passing between them. That night, it is said, Martin dreamed of Jesus wearing the half-cloak. He made no speech about it; he simply saw a cold man and shared what he had.
lent.psalmNote: In ancient Israel the poor had no safety net beyond their neighbours, and the law told farmers to leave grain at the edges of their fields for them. This psalm calls the person who notices the poor blessed, or truly happy. Generosity begins before the giving, with the decision to see the person in front of you.
lent.prayer: Generous God, you see every person nobody else notices. Open my eyes to someone in need today, and loosen my grip on what I have. Let me give quietly, without needing thanks or credit, and find that I am the richer for it. Amen.

lent.title: Lent: Coming Home
lent.line: The story of the prodigal son: however far we wander, the Father runs to meet us.

psalm.text: Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness.

reading.text: While he was still far off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.

midday.text: Return to me, and I will return to you.

evening.text: As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us.

lent.intention: Is there a relationship you need to come home to? Take one step.
lent.ideaLine: However far you have wandered, the door is open.
lent.look: Murillo paints the moment of return. The son kneels barefoot in rags, hands clasped at his chest, not even sure he will be let in. The old father bends over him. Look to the left: a man and a boy are already leading in a calf. That is the fatted calf from the story, brought out for a feast. The welcome was prepared before the apology was finished. The door was never really shut.
lent.psalmNote: Christians have long linked this psalm with King David, who prayed it after his affair with Bathsheba and the death he arranged to cover it. He does not argue his case. He appeals to God’s loving kindness, the Hebrew word for a love that refuses to let go. That is the only ground anyone has for coming home: not our record, but the Father’s love.
lent.prayer: Merciful God, I have wandered further than I meant to, in small ways and some larger ones. Thank you that you watch the road for me. Give me the courage to turn round today, and the humility to be welcomed without earning it. Amen.

lent.title: Lent: The Way of the Cross
lent.line: On Fridays in Lent, Christians walk in their minds the road Jesus walked to the cross.

psalm.text: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?

reading.text: He humbled himself, becoming obedient to death, yes, the death of the cross.

midday.text: Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing.

evening.text: By his wounds we are healed.

lent.intention: Carry someone else's burden today: a chore, a worry, a hard conversation.
lent.look: Turner painted keelmen on the River Tyne at Newcastle, loading coal onto ships through the night. The working boats and ships are dark shapes on either side, and the moon pours a pale, yellow light down the middle of the water. These were hard, heavy jobs done in the dark so the ships could sail with the morning tide. Turner lets the moonlight fall on them without hiding the labour. Today Christians remember Jesus carrying a cross, and that light still falls on everyone doing the heavy lifting for others while no one is watching.
lent.psalmNote: These are the words Jesus cried from the cross, and they open Psalm 22. The psalm was written by someone in agony who felt utterly abandoned, yet kept speaking to God anyway. It moves slowly from despair towards trust. That Jesus prayed it tells us no burden, not even the feeling that God has gone, is outside his reach.
lent.prayer: My God, when I feel forsaken, you have been there before me. Jesus carried his cross all the way and did not put it down. Give me the strength to carry what is mine without complaint, and eyes to see whose load I could lift today, quietly, and without needing thanks. Amen.

lent.title: Lent: Waiting
lent.line: Lent teaches us to wait, and to trust in the dark.

psalm.text: I wait for the Lord. My soul waits. I hope in his word.

reading.text: It is good that a man should hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the Lord.

midday.text: Wait for the Lord. Be strong, and let your heart take courage.

evening.text: Into your hands I commend my spirit.

lent.intention: What are you waiting for in your life? Hand it to God tonight.
lent.ideaLine: Some things can only be waited for. Trust in the dark.
lent.look: Inness fills most of this canvas with dark woods, tall trunks crowding out the sky. Then a shaft of warm evening light breaks through from the left and lands on one pale trunk and a patch of mossy ground. It doesn’t clear the darkness; it simply reaches into it. That is what waiting in faith often feels like. The wood stays dark for a long time, and the light comes in its own hour, often onto something small. You do not make it arrive. You stay, and you watch for it.
lent.psalmNote: This psalm begins “Out of the depths”, and it was sung by pilgrims climbing towards Jerusalem. The next verse compares the soul to watchmen waiting for morning: they can do nothing to hurry the dawn, but they know it is coming. That is the waiting Lent teaches, honest about the dark and sure of the light.
lent.prayer: Lord, I am not good at waiting. I want answers now, and the dark makes me restless. Teach me to wait for you the way a night watchman waits for morning, not anxiously, but trusting that dawn is on its way. Hold what I cannot yet see resolved. Amen.

advent.title: Advent: Hope
advent.line: The first week of Advent: in the darkest time of the year, we wait for the light.

psalm.text: I wait for the Lord. My soul waits. I hope in his word.

reading.text: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light.

midday.text: May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing.

evening.text: Guide me in your truth, and teach me, for you are the God of my salvation.

advent.intention: Where do you need hope? Bring a little of it to someone else today.
advent.ideaLine: In the darkest time of the year, we wait for the light.
advent.look: The angel Gabriel has come to tell Mary she will bear a child, and if you look closely you can see their words painted in gold letters between them. Mary’s reply is written upside down, so that it can be read from heaven. She listens with hands raised, holding nothing yet but a promise, while a beam of light falls through the high window behind her. Hope is like this: a yes given to God before we can see how things will turn out, while the light is only just coming in.
advent.psalmNote: This psalm begins “out of the depths”, and it was sung by pilgrims climbing up to Jerusalem. The writer knows failure and darkness, yet he waits for God the way a night watchman waits for morning, sure it will come. Hope here is not a mood but a way of waiting, with your face towards the dawn.
advent.prayer: Lord, the days are short and the nights are long, and some of what I hope for feels far off. Teach me to wait for you as a watchman waits for morning. Let your word be my light, and let me carry a little of it to someone else today. Amen.

advent.title: Advent: Peace
advent.line: The second week of Advent: waiting for the Prince of Peace.

psalm.text: Mercy and truth meet together. Righteousness and peace have kissed each other.

reading.text: For to us a child is born. His name shall be called Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.

midday.text: Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you.

evening.text: They shall beat their swords into ploughshares.

advent.intention: Where could you make peace this week: at home, at work, in yourself?
advent.ideaLine: Peace begins small: at home, at work, inside yourself.
advent.look: Bassano sets the first Christmas announcement not in a palace but at the bottom of a steep hill, among cows, sheep, a goat and a dog. Five shepherds kneel, sit and lounge as if it were any ordinary evening. Then, in the upper half, an angel appears in a shaft of golden light. Peace arrives here first, among working people and their animals. It still does. It rarely begins with world leaders. It begins where we already are, at the kitchen table or the office desk.
advent.psalmNote: This psalm was prayed by people who had come home from exile to a damaged land and a fragile peace. The poet pictures four great qualities meeting like old friends: mercy with truth, justice with peace, embracing. In real life they are often at odds. Advent hopes for a peace that does not cost the truth, and a justice that is not cruel.
advent.prayer: God of peace, let mercy and truth meet in me today. Where I am tempted to win an argument, help me keep the friendship. Where I am tempted to smooth things over, give me the courage to be honest. Bring your peace into one small place through me. Amen.

advent.title: Advent: Joy
advent.line: The third week of Advent, traditionally called Gaudete: Rejoice!

psalm.text: The Lord has done great things for us, and we are glad.

reading.text: My soul magnifies the Lord. My spirit has rejoiced in God my Saviour.

midday.text: Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, Rejoice!

evening.text: The desert shall rejoice and blossom like a rose.

advent.intention: Notice three joys today, and share one of them.
advent.ideaLine: Joy is deeper than happiness. Notice it today.
advent.look: This is a tondo, a round painting, and the circle seems to hold mother and child close together. Mary kneels with her arms crossed over her chest and her face tipped down towards the baby lying against the hay. Nothing dramatic is happening, yet her stillness says everything: this is wonder, the kind of gladness that makes you go quiet rather than loud. That is the joy Advent points to. It is deeper than happiness because it rests on a gift received, not on things going our way.
advent.psalmNote: Psalm 126 was sung by people who had come home from exile in Babylon. They remembered the day of their return as being like a dream, their mouths full of laughter. “The Lord has done great things for us” is the voice of people who know joy is a gift, not something they earned. Looking back with gratitude makes room for joy now.
advent.prayer: Lord, you have done great things for me, more than I usually stop to notice. Open my eyes today to the joys hidden in the ordinary, and keep me from waiting for perfect circumstances before I let myself be glad. Like Mary, let me hold your gifts with wonder. Amen.

advent.title: Advent: Love
advent.line: The last week of Advent: Mary says yes, and love comes into the world.

psalm.text: Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good; for his loving kindness endures forever.

reading.text: Behold, the servant of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.

midday.text: We love, because he first loved us.

evening.text: For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son.

advent.intention: Who needs to feel loved before Christmas? Tell them.
advent.ideaLine: Who needs to feel loved before the year turns?
advent.look: Raphael sets a mother and two small boys in a quiet landscape, inside a perfect circle. The second child is John the Baptist, and he is offering the infant Jesus a little cross made of reeds. Look where the eyes go: all three of them are on that cross. Even here, in the gentlest of scenes, love is already reaching towards what it will cost. Mary said yes knowing only a little of that. Real love tends to say yes before it knows everything.
advent.psalmNote: This was a song for worship in the Temple, with the second line repeated after every verse like a chorus: his loving kindness endures forever. The Hebrew word is hesed, a loyal, covenant love that does not give up. At the end of Advent, it is the love Christians believe came into the world as a child.
advent.prayer: God whose loving kindness never runs out, thank you for loving me before I ever turned towards you. As Christmas comes near, let your love pass through me to someone who needs it. Give me the words, and the nerve, to tell them they matter. Amen.

christmastide.title: Christmastide: God With Us
christmastide.line: The twelve days of Christmas: God has come to live among us.

psalm.text: Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done marvellous things!

reading.text: The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory.

midday.text: They shall call his name Immanuel, which means, God with us.

evening.text: Make a joyful noise to the Lord, all the earth!

christmastide.intention: Who could use a visit or a call during these twelve days?
christmastide.ideaLine: Twelve days of celebration in the depth of winter.
christmastide.look: Mary kneels in the stone ruins of an old building, praying over a thin-limbed baby who lies on the bare ground, while Joseph stands behind and shepherds out in the field hear the news from an angel. Juan de Flandes made the child small and fragile on purpose. The crumbling walls suggest an old world passing away, with something new and vulnerable arriving in the middle of it. This is what Christians celebrate for twelve days: God came not in power, but as a baby on a cold floor.
christmastide.psalmNote: This psalm was sung to celebrate God rescuing his people, and it calls the whole earth, even the sea and the hills, to join in. A “new song” is the response to something that has never happened before. For Christians, a God who becomes a baby is exactly that, and worth twelve days of singing in the depth of winter.
christmastide.prayer: God who came close, you have done marvellous things, and the greatest is that you came to live among us. Put a new song in my mouth today. Let me carry your light into the dark corners of these winter days, and to someone who is alone. Amen.

holyweek.title: Holy Week
holyweek.line: The last week of Jesus' life, as he walks towards the cross.

psalm.text: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?

reading.text: When he came near, he saw the city and wept over it.

midday.text: Not my will, but yours, be done.

evening.text: Into your hands I commend my spirit.

holyweek.intention: Stay close to someone who is suffering this week.
holyweek.ideaLine: Facing suffering honestly, and staying close to those who suffer.
holyweek.look: Grünewald does not look away, and he asks us not to either. The body on the cross is twisted and bloodied, the crown of thorns sharp, the land behind dark and rocky. This is suffering painted without comfort. Yet three people stand there, close enough to touch. By tradition they are Mary his mother, his friend John, and Mary Magdalene. They cannot fix anything. They simply stay. That is often all we can do for someone in pain, and it is a great deal.
holyweek.psalmNote: Psalm 22 is a lament, a prayer from someone who feels utterly abandoned and says so to God’s face. It was in Israel’s prayer book precisely so that people would have words for their worst days. Jesus prayed it from the cross. This week begins by giving us permission to be honest about suffering, ours and other people’s.
holyweek.prayer: God, this week you walk towards the cross with your eyes open. Teach me to do the same with the suffering around me. Keep me from easy words and from looking away. Show me who needs company more than answers, and give me the patience to stay. Amen.

ash-wednesday.title: Ash Wednesday
ash-wednesday.line: Lent begins. "Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return."

psalm.text: Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. Create in me a clean heart.

reading.text: Tear your heart and not your garments, and turn to the Lord your God; for he is gracious and merciful.

midday.text: For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.

evening.text: As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us.

ash-wednesday.intention: Choose your Lent: one thing to give up, one thing to take up, one person to give to.
ash-wednesday.ideaLine: A day to face our limits honestly, and begin again.
ash-wednesday.look: Bosch shows a man on his deathbed in the moment that matters most. Death, a skeleton, comes through the door with an arrow. An angel at the man’s side points him up towards a crucifix in the window, while a small demon offers him a bag of gold. At the foot of the bed, a figure stores coins in a chest, as if he had spent his life on it; even now, the man has to choose where to look. Ash Wednesday asks the same question, while there is still time: what are you holding on to, and where are you looking?
ash-wednesday.psalmNote: Psalm 51 is traditionally linked to King David after he had taken another man’s wife and arranged her husband’s death. It is the prayer of someone who has stopped making excuses. He does not ask for a tidier reputation but for a clean heart, a new start from the inside. On the first day of Lent, it gives us honest words to begin with.
ash-wednesday.prayer: Merciful God, I am dust, and I know it better than I like to admit. I bring you what I have done and failed to do, without excuses. Create a clean heart in me, and show me this Lent what to let go of, and what to take up instead. Amen.

palm-sunday.title: Palm Sunday
palm-sunday.line: Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a donkey, and the crowds wave palms.

psalm.text: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!

reading.text: Hosanna to the son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!

midday.text: Your King comes to you, humble, and riding on a donkey.

evening.text: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?

palm-sunday.intention: Welcome Jesus into the week ahead: what would you like him to find?
palm-sunday.ideaLine: Real authority rides in on a donkey, not a warhorse.
palm-sunday.look: This is not the entry into Jerusalem but what came just before it. People in flowing robes of pink, teal and gold crowd round a cave in the hills, some pointing, as a man appears at its mouth: Lazarus, called back from death. John’s Gospel says that is why the crowds came out with palms: they had heard what happened at Bethany. Strange, then, that the one who could do this chose a donkey. His power was real, and he wore it lightly.
palm-sunday.psalmNote: Pilgrims sang this psalm as they arrived at the Temple, and priests answered with a blessing for each one who came. On Palm Sunday the crowd sang it to Jesus, welcoming him as the one sent by God. It frames today’s idea: the king they blessed came humbly, as a guest.
palm-sunday.prayer: Blessed are you, Lord Jesus, who came not on a warhorse but on a donkey. Come into my week the same way, quietly and close. Where I want to be impressive, make me humble. Where I want to control, let me welcome you instead, and find your way better than mine. Amen.

maundy-thursday.title: Maundy Thursday
maundy-thursday.line: The Last Supper, when Jesus washed his friends' feet and gave the new commandment: love one another.

psalm.text: What will I give to the Lord for all his benefits toward me? I will take the cup of salvation.

reading.text: If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet.

midday.text: A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another.

evening.text: Not my will, but yours, be done.

maundy-thursday.intention: Do one humble, hidden act of service for someone today.
maundy-thursday.ideaLine: The greatest leader washes his friends' feet.
maundy-thursday.look: Blake seats thirteen people around one long table and bathes them all in the same golden light, skin, clothes and table alike. No one is left in shadow, not even the friend who will betray Jesus before the night is out. This is the meal at which Jesus knelt and washed his friends’ feet, a slave’s task. Blake does not show that moment, but his light says the same thing: everyone at this table is loved, and the greatest among them has come to serve.
maundy-thursday.psalmNote: This is a thanksgiving psalm, sung by someone rescued from death. The cup was raised at a festive meal in thanks to God, and Jewish families still sing these psalms at Passover, which is the meal Jesus shared on this night. The question it asks is simple: when you have been given so much, what can you give back?
maundy-thursday.prayer: Lord Jesus, you knelt to wash your friends’ feet, even the one who would betray you. I have received more than I can repay. Show me one small, hidden way to serve someone today, and take away my wish to be seen doing it. Amen.

good-friday.title: Good Friday
good-friday.line: The day Jesus died on the cross. Christians call it good, because of what it won.

psalm.text: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?

reading.text: He was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.

midday.text: It is finished.

evening.text: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!

good-friday.intention: Keep an hour of quiet today, perhaps between noon and three, when Jesus hung on the cross.
good-friday.ideaLine: The day the world remembers the ultimate sacrifice.
good-friday.look: Perugino paints the crucifixion very differently from most. The scene is strangely calm: Mary stands at the foot of the cross on one side, John on the other, and behind them a deep, peaceful landscape of mountains and a winding river. There is little blood. Perugino seems to be showing us what the cross means rather than how it hurt. The world carries on, wide and beautiful, and at the very centre of it a love that held nothing back.
good-friday.psalmNote: When Jesus cried out these words on the cross, he was quoting the opening line of Psalm 22. Anyone who knew the psalm would know it does not end in despair; by its close the writer is praising God, who “has not hidden his face”. On Good Friday Christians hold both: real abandonment, and a love that goes through it to the end.
good-friday.prayer: Jesus, on this day you went all the way down into loss and loneliness, so that no one would be there alone again. I don’t fully understand it. I can stay near and be grateful. Let your love that went to the end reach someone today through me. Amen.

holy-saturday.title: Holy Saturday
holy-saturday.line: The day of silence, when Jesus lay in the tomb and the world waited.

psalm.text: I wait for the Lord. My soul waits. I hope in his word.

reading.text: Joseph took the body, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth, and laid it in his own new tomb.

midday.text: It is good that a man should hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the Lord.

evening.text: In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep.

holy-saturday.intention: Sit with the silence today. Grief and waiting are part of faith too.
holy-saturday.ideaLine: A day of waiting, when nothing seems to happen.
holy-saturday.look: Here the body of Jesus is carried on a cloth towards the tomb, with the stone structure on the right. Nine people gather around him, faces bowed, and Fra Angelico gives them gold halos even in their grief. Notice the care with which they hold the cloth: this is what love looks like when there is nothing left to do but carry and wait. Holy Saturday is that day. Nothing seems to happen, and yet Christians believe God was at work in the silence, in a way no one could yet see.
holy-saturday.psalmNote: Psalm 130 begins “Out of the depths” and is a cry from someone in deep trouble. It does not describe a rescue. It describes waiting, like a night watchman longing for the morning. Christians pray it on Holy Saturday because it gives words to hope when there is no sign yet that anything will change.
holy-saturday.prayer: Lord, today I wait, as your friends waited by a sealed tomb. I do not have to pretend that grief is not grief, or that the silence is not hard. Hold me in it. Let my soul wait for you, and keep a small hope alive in me until morning. Amen.

easter.title: Easter Day
easter.line: Christ is risen! The heart of the Christian faith.

psalm.text: This is the day that the Lord has made. We will rejoice and be glad in it!

reading.text: He is not here, for he has risen, just like he said.

midday.text: Death, where is your sting? Hades, where is your victory?

evening.text: I am the resurrection and the life.

easter.intention: Share the joy: send an Easter greeting to someone you haven’t spoken to in a while.
easter.ideaLine: The claim at the heart of the West: death is not the end.
easter.look: Behind Jesus is the opening of a tomb cut into rock, and he is standing in front of it, not inside it. Benvenuto paints him calm, a gold halo round his head, a lavender cloth over one shoulder, and a deep landscape running away behind him. The tomb is the past now; the open world is ahead. That is the whole Easter claim in one picture. Death was real, and it was entered. But it is not where the story stays.
easter.psalmNote: This psalm was sung at the Temple to celebrate a rescue that seemed impossible: a stone rejected by the builders becomes the cornerstone. Christians have prayed it on Easter morning for centuries, hearing in it the day God turned defeat into victory. It invites gladness, not because life is easy, but because death does not have the last word.
easter.prayer: Risen Lord, this is the day you have made, and I want to be glad in it. Roll back whatever stone sits on my heart. Let the joy of your rising reach me where I am, and through me reach someone who has not heard from me in far too long. Amen.

ascension.title: Ascension Day
ascension.line: Forty days after Easter, Jesus returns to the Father, promising to be with us always.

psalm.text: God has gone up with a shout, the Lord with the sound of a trumpet.

reading.text: While they were looking, he was taken up, and a cloud received him out of their sight.

midday.text: I am with you always, even to the end of the age.

evening.text: You will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses.

ascension.intention: Jesus sent his friends out. Where are you being sent?
ascension.ideaLine: What you have received is meant to be shared.
ascension.look: Thirteen people kneel on the ground, gazing up at Jesus as he rises on a dark cloud into a sky of shining gold. The painter divides the picture in two, with heaven above in gold and, below, a mossy rock and the earth his friends still stand on. It is natural to keep staring at the sky, but in the story two strangers ask them why they are standing there looking up. Their work is down here now, and what they have seen they are meant to carry into the world.
ascension.psalmNote: This psalm was probably sung in a festival procession as God’s presence, symbolised by the ark (a sacred chest), was carried up into the Temple with shouting and trumpets. It is a coronation song. Christians read it on Ascension Day because Jesus goes up as king, and kings send out messengers.
ascension.prayer: Risen Lord, you have gone up, yet you promised to be with us always. Lift my eyes to you, then set my feet on the ground. Show me where you are sending me today, and give me something worth sharing when I get there. Amen.

pentecost.title: Pentecost
pentecost.line: The Holy Spirit comes like wind and fire, and the Church is born.

psalm.text: You send out your Spirit and they are created. You renew the face of the ground.

reading.text: Suddenly there came from the sky a sound like the rushing of a mighty wind, and tongues like fire appeared, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit.

midday.text: The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.

evening.text: Come, Holy Spirit.

pentecost.intention: Pick one fruit of the Spirit to practise today: patience, kindness or gentleness.
pentecost.ideaLine: The day a small, frightened group found courage.
pentecost.look: Monet painted the front of Rouen Cathedral more than thirty times, in every kind of weather and hour. Here, in sunlight, the heavy stone almost melts into dabs of sky blue, cream, gold and pale pink, as if you were seeing it reflected in a puddle. The building is the same as yesterday. The light has changed everything about it. That is a good picture of Pentecost: the same frightened friends of Jesus, suddenly alight, and the Church becoming living people rather than stone.
pentecost.psalmNote: This psalm is a long hymn of praise for creation, from mountains and springs to lions and the sea. In Hebrew the word for Spirit is also the word for breath and wind. The psalmist sees God breathing life into the world over and over, renewing it. At Pentecost Christians believe the same breath blew through a small room and made the Church.
pentecost.prayer: Spirit of God, breath and fire, blow through the stale places in me today. Where I am timid, give me courage. Where I am tired, renew me as you renew the face of the earth. Let someone meet a little more patience and kindness because you are at work. Amen.

trinity.title: Trinity Sunday
trinity.line: One God in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, a communion of love.

psalm.text: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty.

reading.text: Go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

midday.text: God is love.

evening.text: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, God's love, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.

trinity.intention: God is a relationship of love. Invest in one of yours today.
trinity.ideaLine: The idea that reality, at its heart, is a relationship of love.
trinity.look: Memling sets Mary and the child under a carved stone arch, with an angel kneeling on each side. Everyone in the picture is turned towards the child, and the scene is full of calm, attentive care. It is a circle of love with a gift at its centre. Christians believe God is like that at the deepest level: not a lonely power but Father, Son and Holy Spirit, a love that is always giving itself away. The painting doesn’t show the Trinity, but it hints at its shape: love gathered round, and opening outwards to us.
trinity.psalmNote: These words come from Revelation, where a vision of heaven shows creatures who never stop calling God “holy” three times over. Christians have long heard in the threefold “holy” a hint of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Holiness here means otherness: God is greater than we can picture, and yet the centre of all things is love.
trinity.prayer: Holy God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, you are greater than anything I can picture, and yet at your heart is love. Draw me into that love today. Let it show in how I treat the people closest to me, especially the one I most often take for granted. Amen.

01-01.title: New Year: The Naming of Jesus
01-01.line: A new year, and the day Jesus was named. His name means 'God saves'.

psalm.text: So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.

reading.text: You shall call his name Jesus, for it is he who shall save his people from their sins.

midday.text: Behold, I am making all things new.

evening.text: His compassion doesn't fail. It is new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.

01-01.intention: Instead of a resolution, choose one way to build something good this year.
01-01.ideaLine: Instead of a resolution, choose one good thing to build.
01-01.look: A baby sets off on a river in a golden boat, surrounded by flowers, while an angel stands behind him with a hand on the tiller. It is the first of Thomas Cole’s four paintings of a whole human life, and the boat’s prow holds an hourglass. Time has started running, but the child is not steering alone. That is a good way into a new year: not a list of resolutions, but trust that you are guided, and a choice about what to build with the hours you are given.
01-01.psalmNote: This prayer is the only psalm credited to Moses. It sets our short lives against God’s eternity, not to depress us, but to make us wise. To count our days is to know they are limited and precious. On New Year’s Day, it turns an ordinary calendar into a question about what to build.
01-01.prayer: God of every year, my days are numbered and in your hands. Teach me to count them wisely. Instead of grand resolutions, help me choose one good thing to build this year, and give me patience to build it day by day, with you at the tiller. Amen.

01-06.title: The Epiphany
01-06.line: The wise men follow a star and find the Christ child: God revealed to the whole world.

psalm.text: Arise, shine; for your light has come, and the Lord's glory has risen on you.

reading.text: When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. They offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.

midday.text: I am the light of the world.

evening.text: The heavens declare the glory of God.

01-06.intention: The wise men followed a star. What is drawing you towards God?
01-06.ideaLine: What is drawing you towards something greater?
01-06.look: This round painting is crowded with people who wind down from the rocky mountain at the top, along the path and through the ruins, until at last they kneel before a mother and baby at the bottom. Look for the peacock perched on the stable roof, which in the painters’ day was a sign of eternal life. The long, curving procession is the point: nobody arrives all at once. The wise men came a great distance following one light, and it led them somewhere smaller and more surprising than they expected.
01-06.psalmNote: These words from Isaiah were spoken to Jerusalem after exile, a city in ruins, promising light rising over it so brightly that nations and kings would come to see. Christians hear that promise coming true when foreign travellers, the wise men, arrive with gifts. The light was always meant for everyone.
01-06.prayer: Lord, your light has risen, and I want to follow it, even when I do not know where the road goes. Give me the curiosity of the wise men and their patience over a long journey. When I find you, let me bring you what I have. Amen.

02-02.title: Candlemas
02-02.line: Forty days after Christmas, the baby Jesus is presented in the Temple, and old Simeon sees the light of the world.

psalm.text: The Lord is my light and my salvation.

reading.text: Now you are releasing your servant, Master, in peace; for my eyes have seen your salvation, a light for revelation to the nations.

midday.text: The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn't overcome it.

evening.text: In your light we will see light.

02-02.intention: Light a candle today, and pray for someone who is in a dark place.
02-02.ideaLine: Light a candle for someone in a dark place.
02-02.look: Zurbarán’s young woman is Saint Lucy, whose name comes from the Latin for light. She holds a palm frond, the old sign of a martyr, and on a pewter plate a pair of eyes, recalling the old legend of how she lost her eyes. It is a startling image, but she stands calmly, lit against the dark. Christians have long asked Lucy to pray for those who cannot see. On a day about light for the world, she reminds us that light is for people in the dark.
02-02.psalmNote: Psalm 27 is a song of confidence written by someone surrounded by enemies and danger. It begins not with the threat but with this short line. Light was precious in a world without electricity, where night meant real danger. Old Simeon, holding the baby Jesus in the Temple, saw the light he had waited for all his life.
02-02.prayer: Lord, you are my light. Thank you for every bit of brightness that has reached me through other people. Today I hold before you someone in a dark place. Let your light find them, and if I can carry a small flame to them myself, show me how. Amen.

03-17.title: St Patrick
03-17.line: The patron saint of Ireland, once a slave there, who went back to bring the gospel.

psalm.text: The Lord is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer.

reading.text: Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ in me, Christ beneath me, Christ above me.

midday.text: Go and make disciples of all nations.

evening.text: I will both lay myself down in peace and sleep.

03-17.intention: Patrick returned to the people who had enslaved him. Who could you show unexpected grace to?
03-17.ideaLine: A former slave returns to show grace to those who enslaved him.
03-17.look: Raphael shows Saint George in armour on a white horse, driving his lance down at a lizard-like dragon, while a princess kneels in prayer in the landscape behind. It is a picture of courage, but notice how calm George’s face is, and how lightly the halo sits above him. Patrick’s courage was of a different kind from a fight. Captured as a teenager and enslaved in Ireland, he escaped, then chose to go back to the people who had held him. Sometimes the bravest thing is not to slay the dragon, but to return with grace.
03-17.psalmNote: Psalm 18 is a song of thanks from someone who had been surrounded by enemies and rescued. A rock and a fortress were the safest places an ancient traveller could find: high ground, thick walls. To call God a rock is to say: when everything else gives way, this holds. Patrick could go back to Ireland because he stood on that rock.
03-17.prayer: Christ, be with me, before me, behind me, in me. Be my rock today when I am tempted to settle old scores. Give me Patrick’s courage, not to win but to go back with grace, and to be kind to someone who has not been kind to me. Amen.

03-25.title: The Annunciation
03-25.line: The angel Gabriel visits Mary, and she says yes to God.

psalm.text: My soul magnifies the Lord.

reading.text: Behold, the servant of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.

midday.text: For nothing spoken by God is impossible.

evening.text: The Word became flesh, and lived among us.

03-25.intention: What is God asking you to say yes to?
03-25.ideaLine: Some of life's greatest turns begin with a simple yes.
03-25.look: Two figures fill this tall panel. The angel Gabriel stands to the left, one arm raised as he speaks. Mary sits to the right in a deep royal-blue dress, the colour painters often gave her. Nothing much is happening, outwardly: no crowd, no drama, two people and a conversation. Yet everything turns on her answer. Many of the great turns of a life look like this, quiet, private, easily missed, and resting on a simple yes.
03-25.psalmNote: These are Mary’s own words, from the song she sang after the angel’s visit, later known as the Magnificat. It is not a psalm, but it is full of the psalms she grew up praying. To “magnify” is to make bigger: her yes makes room for God to be larger in her life.
03-25.prayer: God who asks and does not force, I am often slow to say yes to you. Give me Mary’s courage today. Where you are inviting me into something new, let my soul make room for you, so that you grow larger in my life and my worries grow smaller. Amen.

06-09.title: St Columba
06-09.line: The Irish monk who founded the monastery on Iona in 563 and brought the gospel to Scotland.

psalm.text: The earth is the Lord's, with its fullness.

reading.text: Go into all the world, and preach the Good News to the whole creation.

midday.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news.

evening.text: The Lord will keep your going out and your coming in.

06-09.intention: Columba made a small island a light to a nation. Where is your 'Iona', the place you could shine?
06-09.ideaLine: How a monastery on Iona became a light to a nation.
06-09.look: A young man and three boys lean back in a small sailboat as it tips into a choppy green sea, the sail full of wind. Homer painted this in the years after the American Civil War, and it has a sense of fresh air and possibility. Columba also set out in a small boat, sailing from Ireland with twelve companions to the island of Iona in 563. Most great things begin like this: a few people in a small vessel, trusting the wind, heading for somewhere modest that will matter more than they know.
06-09.psalmNote: This psalm was probably sung as worshippers approached the Temple gates, and it begins by claiming everything: the earth and all that fills it belong to God. For Columba, that meant no island was too remote and no people too far away. Wherever you are today is part of the Lord’s earth.
06-09.prayer: Lord of land and sea, the whole earth is yours, including the small corner where I live and work. Give me Columba’s courage to set out, and his patience to stay. Make the ordinary place I am today a small light for someone else. Amen.

06-24.title: The Birth of John the Baptist
06-24.line: The forerunner, who pointed away from himself to Jesus.

psalm.text: Create in me a clean heart, O God.

reading.text: He must increase, but I must decrease.

midday.text: Make ready the way of the Lord!

evening.text: You, child, will be called a prophet of the Most High.

06-24.intention: Point attention away from yourself today: praise someone else's work.
06-24.ideaLine: Greatness that steps aside for something greater.
06-24.look: Jacopo del Sellaio shows John the Baptist alone on a rocky hill, in a pale blue tunic with jagged edges, a pink cloak over his shoulders. The rough, ragged hem is a reminder of the desert prophet who lived on locusts and wild honey. Yet look how slight and still he is. John drew crowds, and could have built a following of his own. Instead his whole life was a gesture towards someone else. Real greatness sometimes looks like stepping aside.
06-24.psalmNote: Christians have long linked this psalm with King David, who prayed it after a serious wrong. The Hebrew word for “create” here is the one Genesis uses for God making the world from nothing. The writer knows he cannot tidy himself up; he needs something new. John the Baptist’s message was the same: turn round, and make room.
06-24.prayer: God, make in me a clean heart, free of the need to be noticed. Let me be glad when others shine. Give me the grace to point beyond myself today, to praise what someone else has done, and to find my own worth in you rather than in applause. Amen.

06-29.title: Saints Peter and Paul
06-29.line: The fisherman and the former persecutor: two very different men, both martyrs in Rome.

psalm.text: Their voice has gone out through all the earth.

reading.text: I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith.

midday.text: You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly.

evening.text: My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.

06-29.intention: Peter failed and was restored; Paul was turned around. Who deserves a second chance from you?
06-29.ideaLine: A failed fisherman and a former persecutor changed the world.
06-29.look: This panel comes from a small folding altarpiece made in Florence, whose side wings swing open like shutters to show a saint standing in each, either side of Mary and her child. On the left is Peter, grey-haired and bearded, in long robes against gold: the fisherman who denied three times that he even knew Jesus. Yet here he stands in glory, next to the one he had let down, because failure is not the last word. Peter and Paul both became who they were because they were given a second chance.
06-29.psalmNote: Psalm 19 says the sky itself speaks of God without words: its voice goes out through all the earth. Christians later applied the line to the first apostles, whose message spread across the Roman world. Peter the fisherman and Paul the former persecutor were unlikely voices. The psalm suggests that God’s message has a way of travelling through the most unexpected people.
06-29.prayer: Lord, you did not give up on Peter when he failed, or on Paul when he fought against you. Thank you for every second chance I have been given. Make me generous with second chances today, and let my life, flaws and all, carry something of your voice. Amen.

07-22.title: St Mary Magdalene
07-22.line: The first witness of the resurrection, called the apostle to the apostles.

psalm.text: My soul thirsts for you, my flesh longs for you.

reading.text: Jesus said to her, "Mary." She turned and said to him, "Rabboni!" which is to say, "Teacher!"

midday.text: I have seen the Lord!

evening.text: Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning.

07-22.intention: Jesus called her by name. Who could you notice and call by name today?
07-22.ideaLine: Being truly seen and known can change everything.
07-22.look: Artemisia Gentileschi paints Mary Magdalene with her eyes closed and her head tipped back, her hands clasped round her knees, her face caught in a sudden light from above. She is not looking at anything. She is being looked at, and she knows it. That is what the Easter garden was like for her: grieving, unable to see clearly, until she heard her own name. Being truly known can feel like light falling on your face.
07-22.psalmNote: This psalm is headed as a prayer of David in the desert of Judah, where thirst is real. He uses that thirst for his longing for God. Mary Magdalene came to the tomb in the same kind of longing, and was met by name. The psalm says our deepest hunger is to be known.
07-22.prayer: God who knows my name, I thirst for you more than I admit. Thank you that I am not a face in a crowd to you. Help me today to see one person properly, to remember their name and use it, so they know they have been noticed. Amen.

08-06.title: The Transfiguration
08-06.line: On a mountain, Jesus' friends see him shining with the glory of God.

psalm.text: In your light we will see light.

reading.text: His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light.

midday.text: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.

evening.text: The heavens declare the glory of God.

08-06.intention: Look for a moment of glory today: in nature, music or a face.
08-06.ideaLine: Look for a moment of radiance today: in nature, music or a face.
08-06.look: Monet painted the Houses of Parliament again and again from across the Thames, in fog, at dawn and at sunset. Here the solid stone towers have become blue silhouettes against a sky of pink, peach and lavender, shimmering in the river below. Nothing about the building has changed; it is the light that has transformed it. That is close to what Jesus’ friends saw on the mountain, the face they knew every day suddenly shining. Glory is often hidden in what is familiar, waiting for the right light.
08-06.psalmNote: This psalm sets two pictures side by side: the darkness of someone who plots evil, and the generosity of God, which is like a fountain and a light. To see “in your light” is to see things as they truly are. The Transfiguration is that moment, when the disciples see Jesus in the light of who he really is.
08-06.prayer: Lord, in your light I see light. Clear my eyes today, so that I notice the glory hidden in ordinary things: in a song, a sky, a familiar face. When I catch a glimpse of it, let me stop, give thanks, and remember it. Amen.

09-29.title: Michaelmas: St Michael and All Angels
09-29.line: The feast of the archangels and the battle of good against evil.

psalm.text: Praise the Lord, all you his angels, who are mighty in strength.

reading.text: There was war in the sky. Michael and his angels made war on the dragon.

midday.text: He will put his angels in charge of you, to guard you in all your ways.

evening.text: The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them.

09-29.intention: Stand up for what is good in one small, concrete way today.
09-29.ideaLine: The old feast of the fight between good and evil.
09-29.look: Rubens paints Daniel among nine lions in an underground den. They are huge and real; you can almost hear them. Daniel sits with his legs crossed and his hands clasped, head tipped back, looking up towards the light. He was thrown in for refusing to stop praying to God. In the story an angel shuts the lions’ mouths. Standing for what is good rarely feels heroic. It often looks like this: staying faithful, looking up, and trusting that you are not alone.
09-29.psalmNote: This verse comes near the end of Psalm 103, a song that piles up reasons to thank God and then calls on angels, and finally all creation, to join in. In the Bible angels are not cute; they are mighty, and their strength is spent doing what is good. Michaelmas asks us to put whatever strength we have to the same use.
09-29.prayer: God of the angels, mighty in goodness, thank you that the fight against evil is not mine alone. Give me courage for one small battle today: a kind word where there was cruelty, a truth where there was a lie. Let me stand where I should stand. Amen.

10-02.title: The Guardian Angels
10-02.line: An old tradition says every person, especially every child, is watched over by an angel.

psalm.text: He will put his angels in charge of you, to guard you in all your ways.

reading.text: See that you don't despise one of these little ones, for in heaven their angels always see the face of my Father.

midday.text: The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them.

evening.text: In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you alone, Lord, make me live in safety.

10-02.intention: Be a guardian for someone today: look out for a child, a neighbour or a colleague.
10-02.ideaLine: Who looks out for you, and who are you looking out for?
10-02.look: Henry Ossawa Tanner, an African American painter who worked in France, painted the Good Shepherd many times. Here the shepherd is hard to make out: a figure beside a flock in front of a small cottage among trees, barely set apart from the dusk around them. Tanner seems to say that care is often like this, quiet and nearly invisible. Whoever has watched over you probably did it without much notice. And you can do the same for someone today, without anyone needing to see.
10-02.psalmNote: Psalm 91 is a prayer of protection, for anyone who feels exposed to danger. It promises that God’s care surrounds us, sending angels to guard our steps. It was never a promise that nothing bad would happen. It is a trust that we are not unwatched, and that care is woven into the world more deeply than we can see.
10-02.prayer: God who watches over us, thank you for the people, seen and unseen, who have looked out for me without my noticing. Let me be part of your care today. Show me the child, the neighbour or the colleague who needs someone on their side, and help me stand there. Amen.

10-04.title: St Francis of Assisi
10-04.line: The rich young man who gave everything away, loved the poor and called the sun his brother.

psalm.text: The earth is the Lord's, with its fullness.

reading.text: Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. Even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these.

midday.text: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven.

evening.text: Let everything that has breath praise the Lord!

10-04.intention: Give away one thing you own but don’t need to someone who will use it.
10-04.ideaLine: The rich young man who gave everything away and called the sun his brother.
10-04.look: In a meadow below jagged mountains, two friars in grey robes look up at a flame-red cross in the sky. One of them is Francis, on the mountain of La Verna in 1224, two years before his death, when tradition says he received wounds like those of Christ. A rich merchant’s son, he had given away everything, and here he has almost nothing left but his robe and his attention. Simplicity, for Francis, was not about having less for its own sake. It left him free to notice God.
10-04.psalmNote: This psalm was probably sung as worshippers came up to the Temple. Its opening sweeps everything in: the earth, all it holds, everyone who lives in it, belongs to God. For Francis this was the root of his joy. If nothing is truly ours, we can hold things lightly, and love them all the more.
10-04.prayer: Lord of the earth and everything in it, nothing I own is really mine. Loosen my grip on what I don’t need. Give me the light heart of Francis, glad in small things, grateful for the world you made, and free enough to share what I have. Amen.

11-01.title: All Saints
11-01.line: The great company of holy men and women, known and unknown, who have gone before us.

psalm.text: Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.

reading.text: Since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us run with perseverance the race that is set before us.

midday.text: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.

evening.text: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes.

11-01.intention: Who has shown you what goodness looks like? Thank them, or thank God for them.
11-01.idea: The people who show us goodness
11-01.ideaLine: Who has shown you what a good life looks like?
11-01.look: An old man with a white beard sits at his table, interrupted, turning his head as an angel appears behind him. This is Jerome, the fourth-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin and was famous for his learning, and also for his temper. Vouet shows him not as a plaster figure but as a real, wrinkled man in shadowy light, caught mid-thought. Saints are not people without faults; they are ordinary people who kept listening, and who show the rest of us what goodness looks like.
11-01.psalmNote: This verse comes from a psalm of thanks sung by someone who had nearly died. It says that God does not treat the death of those who love him as a small thing. Christians on All Saints remember that the good people who have gone before us are not forgotten; each of their lives is precious to God.
11-01.prayer: Lord, thank you for the people who showed me goodness, the famous saints and the quiet ones whose names only you and I know. They were precious to you, and they are precious to me. Help me to run my own race with the same faithfulness. Amen.

11-02.title: All Souls
11-02.line: A day to remember and pray for all who have died.

psalm.text: Out of the depths I have cried to you, Lord.

reading.text: In my Father's house are many homes. I am going to prepare a place for you.

midday.text: I am the resurrection and the life.

evening.text: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more.

11-02.intention: Say the names of those you have lost, aloud, and give thanks for them.
11-02.ideaLine: Say the names of those you have lost, and give thanks for them.
11-02.look: This is the last of Thomas Cole’s four paintings called The Voyage of Life, which follow one traveller from childhood to old age. Now he is an old man in a golden boat, and an angel guides him away from jagged rocks into calm water, towards a shaft of light breaking through the clouds. Notice he is not rowing. Someone else is steering. On All Souls Christians remember the people they have lost, and trust they were carried safely home.
11-02.psalmNote: Psalm 130 is one of the songs pilgrims sang on the way up to Jerusalem. It begins at the very bottom, in the depths, often pictured as deep water. For centuries Christians have prayed it for the dead. It gives grief somewhere to go, and keeps it talking to God rather than to the dark.
11-02.prayer: Lord, out of the depths I bring you the names of those I miss. Thank you for every one of them, for what they gave me and what they were. Hold them in your keeping, and hold me too, until we meet in the place you have prepared. Amen.

11-11.title: Remembrance
11-11.line: We remember those who died in war, and pray for peace.

psalm.text: He makes wars cease to the end of the earth.

reading.text: Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.

midday.text: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.

evening.text: They shall beat their swords into ploughshares.

11-11.intention: Keep the two minutes' silence at 11:00, and pray for a place at war today.
11-11.ideaLine: We remember those who died in war, and long for peace.
11-11.look: Filippino Lippi shows the body of Jesus, held up on the edge of his tomb by Nicodemus, the man who helped bury him, and two angels. His body is heavy and limp, and they bear its weight with great tenderness. This is what remembrance asks of us: to hold the dead with honour and not look away. On a day when we remember those who died in war, the painting reminds us of the one who said there is no greater love than to lay down your life for your friends.
11-11.psalmNote: Psalm 46 was written for a people in a dangerous world, with nations raging around them. It pictures God breaking bows and spears and making wars cease. It is a promise and a longing at once. Christians pray it on Remembrance Day as an act of hope: war is not the final word on the world.
11-11.prayer: God of peace, we remember those who died in war, and those who still grieve them. Make wars cease, to the ends of the earth. Comfort the places at war today, and make me a peacemaker in the small conflicts of my own life. Amen.

11-16.title: St Margaret of Scotland
11-16.line: The 11th-century queen who fed the poor at her own table and built a ferry for pilgrims.

psalm.text: Blessed is he who considers the poor.

reading.text: I was hungry, and you gave me food to eat. I was a stranger, and you took me in.

midday.text: Inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me.

evening.text: Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good.

11-16.intention: Feed someone today: buy a coffee, give to a food bank, invite someone in.
11-16.ideaLine: A medieval queen who fed the poor at her own table.
11-16.look: De Hooch paints an ordinary Dutch courtyard: brick walls, wood panelling, two men sitting at a table, a woman standing to drink from a tall glass. There is no saint here and no great event. That is the point. Margaret was a queen, yet the place she chose to serve was the everyday table, feeding poor people where she herself ate. Kindness rarely needs a grand stage. It happens in yards, kitchens and cafés, at tables like this one.
11-16.psalmNote: This psalm begins with a blessing on anyone who notices the poor and acts. In ancient Israel caring for the poor was part of the law, not an optional extra. Margaret of Scotland took it literally, feeding the hungry at her own table. The verse makes care for others a kind of blessing, not a burden.
11-16.prayer: God who feeds the hungry, you notice those I tend to walk past. Open my eyes and my hands today. Let me share bread, or coffee, or a seat at my table with someone who needs it, and let them leave feeling welcome rather than pitied. Amen.

11-30.title: St Andrew
11-30.line: Patron saint of Scotland, the fisherman who brought his brother to Jesus.

psalm.text: Come, see the works of God.

reading.text: He first found his own brother, Simon, and said to him, "We have found the Messiah!" He brought him to Jesus.

midday.text: Come after me, and I will make you fishers for people.

evening.text: How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the Good News of peace.

11-30.intention: Andrew brought his brother. Who could you invite: to a meal, a conversation, or church?
11-30.ideaLine: Scotland's patron saint, who brought his brother along.
11-30.look: Constable painted Salisbury Cathedral while staying with his close friend John Fisher, who lived in the Close beside it. You can feel that friendship in the picture: the shady lawn, the trees on the left and the great spire rising through the clouds, seen as if on an easy walk. A friend brought him to the place, and he made it his own. Andrew did something similar when he found his brother Simon and simply said, come and see, which is how faith often travels: through friendship rather than argument.
11-30.psalmNote: This psalm invites the whole earth to praise God for rescuing his people, recalling how he led them through the sea. “Come, see” is an invitation, not an argument: look for yourself. It is exactly what Andrew did for his brother, and what any friend can do for another.
11-30.prayer: Lord, Andrew did not preach; he simply brought his brother to you. Give me that same easy warmth. Show me one person I could invite today, to my table, into a real conversation, or to come and see. And let me be a good friend whatever they say. Amen.

12-06.title: St Nicholas
12-06.line: The 4th-century bishop who gave secret gifts to the poor, the real Santa Claus.

psalm.text: Blessed is he who considers the poor.

reading.text: When you do merciful deeds, don't let your left hand know what your right hand does.

midday.text: It is more blessed to give than to receive.

evening.text: God loves a cheerful giver.

12-06.intention: Give a secret gift today, and tell your children the real story of St Nicholas.
12-06.ideaLine: The real story behind Santa Claus: gifts given in secret.
12-06.look: Chardin paints an older girl teaching a younger child to read. She leans over the cupboard, focused on the open book; the little one looks up at her. There is no audience, no reward, no fuss. This is generosity at its quietest: time and patience given to someone smaller, with no one watching. Saint Nicholas, by legend, dropped gold through a window at night so no one would know. The best gifts often look like this girl’s afternoon.
12-06.psalmNote: This psalm begins with a blessing on anyone who “considers” the poor.
