The word means more than giving: it means paying careful attention, thinking about someone’s situation as if it mattered. In ancient Israel the poor were easily overlooked. Secret generosity starts here, in noticing, before any gift is given.
12-06.prayer: God of the poor, open my eyes to the people I usually walk past. Give me a generous heart that does not need thanks. Show me one gift I can give today without anyone knowing, and let the giving itself be enough. Amen.

12-24.title: Christmas Eve
12-24.line: The holy night: waiting at the manger.

psalm.text: The heavens declare the glory of God.

reading.text: She gave birth to her firstborn son. She wrapped him in bands of cloth, and laid him in a feeding trough, because there was no room for them in the inn.

midday.text: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light.

evening.text: Glory to God in the highest, on earth peace, good will toward men.

12-24.intention: Make room tonight: for God, and for anyone without a place to go.
12-24.ideaLine: Who has no room tonight? Make space for someone.
12-24.look: In Piero di Cosimo’s round painting, the baby lies on a slate-blue cloth under the ruins of a building, with Mary, an angel and the young John the Baptist all gazing at him. Painters often set the nativity among ruins: the old world crumbling, and something new being born in the middle of it. There was no room at the inn, so this child begins life in a broken shelter. Christmas Eve says God came where there was little space, and asks us to make room for him and for others.
12-24.psalmNote: Psalm 19 opens by saying that the sky preaches without words, its glory telling of the God who made it. On Christmas Eve Christians remember a night when the heavens spoke with a star and with angels, over a stable. The psalm invites us to look up, and then to look again at the small, hidden place where God chose to arrive.
12-24.prayer: God of the starry night, you came to us when there was no room. Tonight, make room in me: in my plans, my home and my heart. Show me someone who has nowhere to go, and let me make space for them, as Mary and Joseph made space for you. Amen.

12-25.title: Christmas Day
12-25.line: God becomes a child. The Word becomes flesh.

psalm.text: Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done marvellous things!

reading.text: I bring you good news of great joy which will be to all the people. For there is born to you today a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord.

midday.text: The Word became flesh, and lived among us.

evening.text: Glory to God in the highest, on earth peace.

12-25.intention: Who is alone this Christmas? Reach out to them today.
12-25.ideaLine: The story of light coming into the world, in a stable.
12-25.look: Duccio painted this for the great altarpiece of Siena Cathedral. In the centre Mary lies under a simple wooden shelter set into a rocky cave, surrounded by angels. On either side stand the prophets Isaiah and Ezekiel, who lived centuries earlier, holding their prophecies. They are painted into the same picture as the birth they hoped for. Christmas is like that: an old hope, carried a long time, finally arriving in the plainest of places.
12-25.psalmNote: This psalm is a song of joy for the whole earth, calling on seas, rivers and hills to join in because God has come to set things right. A “new song” is fitting when something has happened that the old songs could not quite hold. Christians hear in it the joy of a God born as a child.
12-25.prayer: God who came among us as a child, I sing a new song today. Thank you for not staying distant, but sharing our ordinary life. Let your light reach those who are alone this Christmas, and use me to carry a little of it to one of them. Amen.

12-26.title: St Stephen
12-26.line: The first Christian martyr, who forgave those who killed him. Good King Wenceslas went out on this day to help the poor.

psalm.text: Into your hands I commend my spirit.

reading.text: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit! Lord, don't hold this sin against them!

midday.text: Love your enemies, and pray for those who persecute you.

evening.text: It is more blessed to give than to receive.

12-26.intention: Like Wenceslas, take something to someone in need today.
12-26.ideaLine: Forgiving your enemies, and taking something to someone in need.
12-26.look: Men and horses tumble across a rocky shore, and at the centre Saul lies sprawled on the ground, knocked flat by a light from heaven on the road to Damascus. Why show this on St Stephen’s Day? When Stephen was stoned to death, the young Saul stood by and held the coats of those who threw the stones, while Stephen prayed for his killers to be forgiven. Not long afterwards, Saul became Paul, the greatest of the early Christian messengers. Forgiveness can change more than we will ever see.
12-26.psalmNote: These are words of trust from someone surrounded by enemies, handing their life over to God. Jesus prayed them on the cross, and Stephen echoed them as he died. They turn a terrible moment into an act of trust, and free the heart enough to forgive the very people causing the harm.
12-26.prayer: Lord Jesus, into your hands I put my life today. Free me from the grudges I carry, and help me to pray for anyone who has hurt me. Then send me out, like good King Wenceslas, with something for someone in need. Amen.

easterweek.title: Easter Week: Christ Is Risen
easterweek.line: The week after Easter is one long celebration: the tomb is empty and everything has changed.

psalm.text: This is the day that the Lord has made. We will rejoice and be glad in it!

reading.text: Jesus himself came near, and went with them. Their eyes were opened, and they recognised him.

midday.text: Peace be to you.

evening.text: Stay with us, for it is almost evening, and the day is almost over.

easterweek.intention: The risen Jesus walked with two sad friends. Walk alongside someone who is struggling today.
easterweek.ideaLine: After the darkest day, something unexpected begins.
easterweek.look: Caspar David Friedrich calls this Spring, though snow still lies among the brown ridges rolling back to the horizon. Look closely and you will find two tiny figures standing in all that space. Nothing in the landscape shouts that winter is over. Yet the season has turned. New life often begins like this, quietly, before it can be seen. Like the two sad friends on the road after Easter, we can be walking beside it before we recognise it.
easterweek.psalmNote: Psalm 118 was sung at the great Jewish festivals, including Passover, and may well be among the psalms Jesus sang with his friends on the night before he died. Early Christians read it as pointing to Easter: the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This is the day. Not a memory, but today.
easterweek.prayer: Risen Lord, this is the day you have made, and you are in it. Open my eyes to recognise you walking beside me. Where I see only late snow, show me spring. And let me walk with someone who is struggling, as you walked with your friends. Amen.

0.title: The Resurrection
0.line: Every Sunday is a little Easter: the day Christ rose from the dead.
0.ideaLine: Some happiness fades by Monday. What kind of joy could last through a hard week?

psalm.text: Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning.

reading.text: Therefore you now have sorrow, but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy away from you.

midday.text: Don't be grieved, for the joy of the Lord is your strength.

evening.text: You have put gladness in my heart, more than when their grain and their new wine are increased.

0.intention: What gave you a deep, quiet gladness this week, rather than a quick thrill? Make room for more of it today.
0.look: Gauguin painted this in Pont-Aven, a village in Brittany, where he spent time among people living by older rhythms. Three girls in white headdresses and clogs hold hands in a loose ring in a grassy field. They are not performing, simply dancing together, and their joy is plain, shared and rooted in a place. That is the kind of joy that lasts. It is less a thrill than a bond, and Christians believe the resurrection gives a joy like that, one that no one can take away.
0.psalmNote: Psalm 30 is a song of thanks from someone who had been very ill and had recovered. They remember the night of tears and the morning of relief. Sorrow is real, the psalm admits, but it is not the end of the story. Christians hear in this line the first Easter morning, and every Sunday since.
0.prayer: Lord of the morning, you have turned my mourning into dancing more often than I remember. Thank you for joys that are deeper than a passing thrill. Root me today in the gladness that comes from you, so that it can last through whatever this week brings. Amen.

0.title: The Resurrection
0.line: Every Sunday is a little Easter: the day Christ rose from the dead.
0.ideaLine: Darkness rarely has the last word. Where have you seen light come back?

psalm.text: Light dawns in the darkness for the upright, gracious, merciful, and righteous.

reading.text: The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn't overcome it.

midday.text: Arise, shine; for your light has come, and the Lord's glory has risen on you.

evening.text: Even the darkness doesn't hide from you, but the night shines as the day. The darkness is like light to you.

0.intention: Think of a dark time that eased. Thank someone who helped bring the light back.
0.look: Durand takes us deep into a forest, mossy trunks looming over a narrow brook, and lets a cool morning light filter through the leaves. Look closely and you will see dead branches, broken and sharp, among the living green. The painter doesn’t hide them. The light falls on both. That is what light after dark is usually like. It does not erase what has died. It arrives quietly, and the forest goes on growing around what was broken.
0.psalmNote: This psalm praises the person who lives generously and fairly, and promises that even for them darkness will come, but so will light. It doesn’t pretend good people escape hard times. It says the dark is not final. Every Sunday Christians recall the first Easter dawn, light rising after the darkest day.
0.prayer: God of the morning, light dawns in the darkness because you will it. Thank you for the times the dark lifted when I thought it never would. Make me patient with today’s shadows, and grateful to the people you have used to bring light back to me. Amen.

0.title: The Resurrection
0.line: Every Sunday is a little Easter: the day Christ rose from the dead.
0.ideaLine: Great things often start tiny. What small beginning in your life deserves a little hope?

psalm.text: He who goes out weeping, carrying seed for sowing, will certainly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves.

reading.text: The Kingdom of Heaven is like a grain of mustard seed which a man took, and sowed in his field, which indeed is smaller than all seeds. But when it is grown, it is greater than the herbs and becomes a tree.

midday.text: Indeed, who despises the day of small things?

evening.text: He won't break a bruised reed. He won't quench a dimly burning wick.

0.intention: Plant something small today: a seed, a habit, a kind word. Then leave it to grow.
0.look: A small child stands on a sunny garden path, dwarfed by towering sunflowers in yellow and burnt orange, every one of which began as a seed no bigger than a fingernail. Monet painted this at Vétheuil, where his wife Camille had died less than two years before, and yet the garden is blazing with light. Life came back. Hope often looks like this: small, steady and further along than it seems.
0.psalmNote: This psalm was sung by people returning from exile to a ruined homeland. Sowing seed in hard times was an act of faith that a harvest would come, even through tears. Easter makes the same promise: what goes into the ground in sorrow can come back with joy.
0.prayer: Lord of the harvest, I bring you the small beginnings in my life, some of them sown with tears. Help me to keep planting, and to trust you with the growing. Let me see today one tiny sign that new life is on its way. Amen.

0.title: The Resurrection
0.line: Every Sunday is a little Easter, kept in memory of the morning Christ rose from the dead.
0.ideaLine: When did you last see something the way a child does, as if for the first time?

psalm.text: Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.

reading.text: Most certainly I tell you, whoever will not receive God's Kingdom like a little child, he will in no way enter into it.

midday.text: From the lips of babes and infants you have established strength.

evening.text: I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.

0.intention: Ask a child, or the child you were, one honest question about the world today, and take the answer seriously.
0.look: Chardin catches a young man leaning on a stone window ledge, blowing a large, glistening bubble through a long straw. A small child peers over the ledge, watching. Painters of the time used soap bubbles as a reminder that life is fleeting. But look at the child: completely absorbed, as if nothing in the world mattered more than this bubble. That attention is a kind of wonder. Jesus said we must receive God’s kingdom like a child, eyes wide open.
0.psalmNote: Psalm 131 is one of the shortest psalms, just three verses. A weaned child is no longer crying for milk; it is content just to be with its mother. The psalmist has stopped grasping and straining. Being like a child, in this sense, is not about being naïve. It is about trust that has quietened down enough to look and wonder.
0.prayer: God, still and quieten my restless soul. Let me rest in you like a child with its mother. Give me back the eyes of a child today, to see ordinary things as if for the first time, and to trust you without needing every answer first. Amen.

1.title: The Angels and the Unseen
1.line: Monday keeps the old devotion to the angels: a reminder that we live among more than we can see.
1.ideaLine: Most of what matters goes unnoticed. What would you see if you slowed down and really looked?

psalm.text: Be still, and know that I am God.

reading.text: Moses said, “I will go now, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burned.”

midday.text: Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They don't toil, neither do they spin.

evening.text: I remember you on my bed, and think about you in the night watches.

1.intention: Choose one ordinary thing today, a tree, a face, a cup of tea, and give it two full minutes of your attention.
1.look: Chardin paints a woman preparing a simple meal for someone who is ill: an egg, a loaf, a pan. The light falls from the left onto her hands and the table, and the background drops away into shadow. She is completely absorbed in what she is doing; nothing grand is happening, but her attention turns a small task into an act of love. Chardin, a painter of ordinary things, paid that same attention to every surface. Today asks us to slow down and look like that.
1.psalmNote: Psalm 46 was written for a people who felt the earth shaking beneath them, in war and in disaster. In the middle of the chaos comes a command: be still, and know that I am God. The word for “be still” means to let go, to stop striving. Stillness, the psalm suggests, is the way we start to see what is truly there.
1.prayer: God who is always here, I rush past so much without seeing it. Slow me down today. Let me give real attention to the people and things in front of me, the way you give attention to me. Be still in me, so that I can notice you. Amen.

1.title: The Angels and the Unseen
1.line: Monday keeps the old devotion to the angels: a reminder that we live among more than we can see.
1.ideaLine: Every stranger is someone's whole world. What might you see in the next one you meet?

psalm.text: The Lord preserves the foreigners. He upholds the fatherless and widow.

reading.text: The stranger who lives as a foreigner with you shall be to you as the native-born among you, and you shall love him as yourself; for you lived as foreigners in the land of Egypt.

midday.text: I was a stranger and you took me in.

evening.text: For I am a stranger with you, a foreigner, as all my fathers were.

1.intention: Learn the name of someone you see often but have never spoken to.
1.look: Landseer painted this when he was about eighteen. A traveller lies almost buried in snow, and two great mountain dogs have found him; the large tan-and-white one is right beside him, close to us. These are the famous dogs of the Alpine passes, kept by monks to rescue people lost in the snow. The man is a stranger to them, and it makes no difference. Sometimes kindness arrives from the last place we expect it, and sometimes we are the ones sent.
1.psalmNote: This psalm praises God as the one who keeps faith with the vulnerable: foreigners, orphans, widows. In ancient Israel these were people with no one to speak for them. The psalm says God stands beside them. To welcome a stranger, then, is to share in something God is already doing.
1.prayer: God who watches over the stranger, I was once a stranger to you, and you welcomed me. Help me see the people I walk past as someone’s whole world. Today, give me the courage to speak to one of them, and the grace to learn their name. Amen.

1.title: The Angels and the Unseen
1.line: Monday keeps the old devotion to the angels: a reminder that we live among more than we can see.
1.ideaLine: The night sky has made people wonder for as long as there have been people. When did you last look up?

psalm.text: The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork.

reading.text: For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made.

midday.text: He counts the number of the stars. He calls them all by their names.

evening.text: When I consider your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have ordained, what is man, that you think of him?

1.intention: Tell someone about a moment that once filled you with wonder, and ask them about one of theirs.
1.look: Two windmills stand on a low horizon, backlit by silver moonlight, and a great dark tree fills half the canvas, but most of the picture is sky. Crome painted the flat country around Norwich, where the sky is enormous and people look small beneath it. At night the familiar world goes dim and something larger becomes visible. Looking up has always made people wonder whether there is more to the world than what we can touch.
1.psalmNote: This psalm comes from a people who watched the stars from open hillsides, without city lights. To them the sky was a voice without words, speaking of its maker every day and every night. It opens a simple thought: creation itself might be a message, if we stop and pay attention.
1.prayer: God of the heavens, the sky speaks of you without words. Lift my eyes from what is small and close. Give me a sense of wonder today, and the humility to believe that there is more around me than I can see. Amen.

1.title: The Angels and the Unseen
1.line: Monday remembers the angels, and that the world holds more than we can see.
1.ideaLine: What beautiful thing have you walked past this week without noticing?

psalm.text: One thing I have asked of the Lord, that I will seek after: that I may dwell in the Lord's house all the days of my life, to see the Lord's beauty.

reading.text: He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts.

midday.text: Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They don't toil, neither do they spin, yet I tell you that even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these.

evening.text: Honour and majesty are before him. Strength and beauty are in his sanctuary.

1.intention: Find one beautiful thing today, a face, a building, a few bars of music, and stay with it for two full minutes.
1.look: Van Gogh painted these roses in May 1890 in the hospital at Saint-Rémy, just before he left. At first glance they are white. Stay a moment and the petals fill with colour: hints of denim and aquamarine blue, sage green, mauve, butter yellow. A jug of flowers could hardly be more ordinary, yet he saw a whole world in it, in a hard season of his life. Hidden beauty is like that. It is not usually missing. We are usually in a hurry.
1.psalmNote: The writer of Psalm 27 asks for just one thing: to live near God and to gaze on God’s beauty. In ancient Israel that meant the Temple, with its music, light and gold. Christians believe the same beauty spills into the world, waiting to be noticed by anyone who slows down long enough to look.
1.prayer: God of all beauty, you have made everything beautiful in its time. Slow me down today. Let me notice one thing I would usually rush past, and stay with it long enough to see it properly, and let that small glimpse turn my heart towards you. Amen.

2.title: Turning Around
2.line: Tuesday keeps the old call to repentance: to turn round, face the truth and begin again.
2.ideaLine: Two small words that can mend a great deal. Is there an apology you have been putting off?

psalm.text: Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.

reading.text: I will get up and go to my father, and will tell him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight.”

midday.text: Leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.

evening.text: I acknowledged my sin to you. I didn't hide my iniquity.

2.intention: Say sorry to one person today, plainly, without a ‘but’.
2.look: Luini paints Mary Magdalene looking straight out at us from the corners of her eyes, against an almost black background, her auburn hair falling down her back. For centuries Christians remembered her as a sinner who turned round, though the Bible itself only says Jesus freed her from seven demons. What she certainly did was stay with Jesus at the cross and come first to his tomb. Her gaze here is direct and unashamed. That is what an honest apology can do: let us look the world in the eye again.
2.psalmNote: Psalm 51 is the prayer of someone who has done real wrong and has stopped pretending otherwise. Tradition links it to King David after a terrible abuse of power. He does not ask God for an easier conscience but for a new heart. Saying sorry, the psalm suggests, is not humiliation. It is how something clean begins.
2.prayer: Father, like the son who came home, I need to get up and say sorry. Create in me a clean heart, and give me the words today for one honest apology, without excuses and without a ‘but’. Renew my spirit, so I can begin again. Amen.

2.title: Turning Around
2.line: Tuesday keeps the old call to repentance: to turn round, face the truth and begin again.
2.ideaLine: The hardest person to be truthful with is often yourself. What do you already know but avoid looking at?

psalm.text: Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.

reading.text: Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but don't consider the beam that is in your own eye?

midday.text: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us.

evening.text: Who can discern his errors? Forgive me from hidden errors.

2.intention: Before bed, write down one thing you did today that you are not proud of, and one you are.
2.look: Van Gogh painted this self-portrait in 1889, during his stay in a hospital at Saint-Rémy in the south of France, after one of the hardest years of his life. He looks straight out at us, but of course he was looking at himself in a mirror. The blue smock and background swirl in long strokes, and nothing is flattered. It takes courage to study your own face like that. Being honest with yourself is the same kind of work: looking steadily, without cruelty and without excuses.
2.psalmNote: This psalm marvels that God knows every part of us, our sitting and standing, our words before we speak them. It ends with this request to be searched. To ancient Israel, God’s knowledge was not a threat but a comfort. Being honest with yourself becomes easier when you trust you are already fully known, and still loved.
2.prayer: God who knows me through and through, search me and show me what I would rather not see. Give me courage to look honestly at my own heart, not to condemn myself, but so that you can lead me somewhere better. Amen.

2.title: Turning Around
2.line: Tuesday keeps the old call to repentance: to turn round, face the truth and begin again.
2.ideaLine: Sorry is the start. Is there something you could put right, not just regret?

psalm.text: Depart from evil, and do good. Seek peace, and pursue it.

reading.text: Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.”

midday.text: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does the Lord require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?

evening.text: The Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness.

2.intention: Think of a wrong you have done. Take one practical step today to repair it: return, repay, or rebuild.
2.look: Golden evening light falls across autumn trees and onto a stone church with spires and stained glass, seen from a height as if we are arriving from a long way off. Cole painted it as a pair with a picture called The Departure: morning and setting out, then evening and coming home. Returning is rarely the end of the road, because it is where we face what happened while we were away. Making amends is like this: coming back to the place you left, and putting right what you can.
2.psalmNote: This psalm is credited to David when he was on the run, pretending madness to escape a king. Its wisdom is practical: turning away from wrong is not enough; you must do good and chase peace. The word “pursue” is active, and making amends means going after peace, not just wishing for it.
2.prayer: Lord, I am sorry for the wrongs I have done, and I do not want to stop at being sorry. Give me courage to pursue peace and put right what I can, as Zacchaeus did. Where I cannot repair it, heal what I have damaged. Amen.

2.title: Turning Around
2.line: Tuesday recalls John the Baptist, who called people to turn round and begin again.
2.ideaLine: Where in your life is a small lie doing more harm than the truth would?

psalm.text: Behold, you desire truth in the inward parts. You teach me wisdom in the inmost place.

reading.text: Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak truth each one with his neighbour, for we are members of one another.

midday.text: Lord, who shall dwell in your sanctuary? … He who walks blamelessly and does what is right, and speaks truth in his heart.

evening.text: You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.

2.intention: If you have let a small untruth stand, put it right today with the person concerned, kindly and plainly.
2.look: Judith Leyster turns from her easel and looks straight at us, lips slightly parted, as if about to speak. She was one of the few women admitted to the painters’ guild in Haarlem. Yet for more than two centuries much of her work was credited to Frans Hals, until in the 1890s her monogram was found under his false signature. The truth took a long time to come out, and it gave her back her name. Truth does that: it restores what lies have taken.
2.psalmNote: Christians have long linked this psalm with King David after a serious wrong he had tried to hide. Here he sees that God wants honesty not just in what we say but deep inside, in the places we keep from others and even from ourselves. Telling the truth to others begins with telling it to ourselves first.
2.prayer: God of truth, you see what I keep hidden. Teach me honesty in the inward places. Where I have let a small lie settle, give me the courage to clear it, and the kindness to speak truthfully without wounding. Let my words today be ones others can trust. Amen.

2.title: Turning Around
2.line: Tuesday recalls John the Baptist, who called people to turn round and begin again.
2.ideaLine: Is there an anger you have been feeding that it is time to set down?

psalm.text: Cease from anger, and forsake wrath. Don't fret; it leads only to evildoing.

reading.text: Be angry, and don't sin. Don't let the sun go down on your wrath.

midday.text: Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.

evening.text: Stand in awe, and don't sin. Search your own heart on your bed, and be still.

2.intention: Before you send a sharp message or reply today, wait an hour, then reread it and soften one line.
2.look: Van de Velde, a painter of the sea, shows the moment after the worst has passed. The boats are still tipped at a sharp angle and the waves are still grey and choppy, topped with white foam, under a charcoal sky. But no one is going under: the storm has blown itself out, and the water will settle if it is given time. Anger can be like this. It doesn’t vanish all at once, but it does not have to sink us, and the calm comes back when we stop feeding the wind.
2.psalmNote: Psalm 37 was written for people angry at seeing the wicked prosper while they struggled. Its advice is surprisingly practical: stop fretting, because brooding anger only leads us to do wrong ourselves. It invites a slower trust, that justice is in God’s hands, not ours alone. Setting anger down, the psalm says, is not weakness but freedom.
2.prayer: God of peace, you know the anger I carry and how often I feed it. Help me to set it down today. When I want to strike back, slow my words. Teach me to trust you with what is unfair, and to sleep tonight without a grudge. Amen.

2.title: Turning Around
2.line: Tuesday recalls John the Baptist, who called people to turn round and begin again.
2.ideaLine: When did you last change your mind, and what made it possible?

psalm.text: He will guide the humble in justice. He will teach the humble his way.

reading.text: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does the Lord require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?

midday.text: Whoever loves correction loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof is stupid.

evening.text: Lord, my heart isn't arrogant, nor my eyes lofty; nor do I concern myself with great matters, or things too wonderful for me.

2.intention: Ask someone you trust where they think you might be wrong, and listen to the answer without defending yourself.
2.look: A boy in a dark cap sits forward on a rocking chair, reaching towards the stove, where the half-open door shows a bright orange glow. Eastman Johnson called him The Early Scholar. Notice the posture: leaning in, drawn towards the warmth and light. That is what being teachable looks like. Not a grown-up certainty that has everything sorted, but a child’s readiness to lean towards something and let it change you.
2.psalmNote: This psalm is a prayer for guidance, written as an acrostic, each verse starting with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, like a lesson. Its promise is simple: God teaches those who are humble enough to be taught. Changing your mind, in this light, is not weakness. It is a sign you are still learning.
2.prayer: God who teaches the humble, I would often rather be right than learn. Soften my pride today. When someone shows me I am wrong, help me listen without rushing to defend myself, and give me the grace to change my mind when I should. Amen.

3.title: Keeping Faith
3.line: Wednesday remembers God's faithfulness, and asks for the grace to stay faithful in return.
3.ideaLine: Anyone can start. What helps a person keep going when the shine has worn off?

psalm.text: I waited patiently for the Lord. He turned to me, and heard my cry.

reading.text: We also rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces perseverance; and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope.

midday.text: Let's not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don't give up.

evening.text: Rest in the Lord, and wait patiently for him.

3.intention: What good thing are you tempted to give up on? Do one small piece of it today.
3.look: Men and women work across a field harvesting rapeseed, bending, lifting and carrying in the summer heat. Breton grew up in a farming village in northern France and painted workers like these with respect, never as quaint. There is nothing glamorous here: a harvest is the result of months of steady, unremarkable work, done in all weathers, mostly together. That is what staying power looks like, not a burst of enthusiasm but showing up again tomorrow, alongside others, until the crop is in.
3.psalmNote: The writer remembers a time of desperate waiting, when it felt like being stuck in a muddy pit, and how God finally heard. The Hebrew literally says “waiting, I waited”: a long wait. Faithfulness is often like that, and the psalm promises that patience is not wasted.
3.prayer: Faithful God, you heard the cry of those who waited patiently, even when the wait was long. When the shine wears off the good things I have started, give me the strength to keep going. Let me do one small faithful thing today. Amen.

3.title: Keeping Faith
3.line: Wednesday remembers God's faithfulness, and asks for the grace to stay faithful in return.
3.ideaLine: Loyalty shows when things go wrong. Who has stood by you, and who needs you to stand by them?

psalm.text: Your loving kindness, Lord, is in the heavens. Your faithfulness reaches to the skies.

reading.text: Where you go, I will go; and where you stay, I will stay. Your people will be my people, and your God my God.

midday.text: A friend loves at all times; and a brother is born for adversity.

evening.text: I will sing of the loving kindness of the Lord forever. With my mouth, I will make known your faithfulness to all generations.

3.intention: Get in touch with someone going through a hard patch, and let them know you are still there.
3.look: Berthe Morisot paints two young women side by side on a couch, in matching white dresses with pale blue spots, their dark hair pinned up the same way. They do not look at each other, and they don’t need to. Their closeness is in simply being there, together, shoulder to shoulder. Loyalty often looks like this. Not dramatic rescue, just staying on the same couch when things go wrong, so that the other person never has to wonder if you are still there.
3.psalmNote: Psalm 36 starts with a bleak picture of people who plot harm, then suddenly lifts its eyes. God’s loving kindness and faithfulness are as high as the sky, too large to be spoiled by human failure. Ruth’s promise to stick by Naomi is that same faithfulness brought down to earth, in one person refusing to leave another.
3.prayer: Faithful God, your kindness reaches higher than the skies and you have never walked out on me. Thank you for the people who stood by me when it was hard. Show me who needs me to stand by them now, and make me steady and loyal to them. Amen.

3.title: Keeping Faith
3.line: Wednesday remembers God's faithfulness, and asks for the grace to stay faithful in return.
3.ideaLine: Trust is easy when all is clear. What helps you hold on when you cannot see the way ahead?

psalm.text: Why are you in despair, my soul? Why are you disturbed within me? Hope in God.

reading.text: But those who wait for the Lord will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.

midday.text: When I am afraid, I will put my trust in you.

evening.text: My soul, wait in silence for God alone, for my expectation is from him.

3.intention: Name one worry you cannot fix today. Write it down, and for now, let it rest there.
3.look: Carpaccio shows Joseph leading a donkey carrying Mary and the baby Jesus across a hilly landscape. They are fleeing to Egypt to escape King Herod, who wanted the child dead. They have no clear plan and no way of knowing how long they will be gone. Yet Joseph walks steadily, leaning on his staff, one step at a time. Trust in the dark looks like this: not seeing the whole road, but putting one foot in front of the other, together.
3.psalmNote: Psalm 42 was written by someone far from home and unable to worship as they once had. They argue with their own soul, asking why it is so low, and then tell it to hope in God. It is honest about despair without letting despair have the last word. Trust, the psalm suggests, is something we can speak back to ourselves.
3.prayer: God of the long road, I cannot see the way ahead, and my soul is disturbed in me. Teach me to hope in you anyway. Like Joseph, let me take the next step without needing to see the whole route, and give me strength to keep walking. Amen.

3.title: Keeping Faith
3.line: Wednesday is for faithfulness: God's to us, and ours to God and to each other.
3.ideaLine: What would change if you did today's ordinary work as if it mattered?

psalm.text: Let the favour of the Lord our God be on us. Establish the work of our hands for us.

reading.text: And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men.

midday.text: Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might.

evening.text: It is vain for you to rise up early, to stay up late, eating the bread of toil, for he gives sleep to his loved ones.

3.intention: Pick one dull task today and do it carefully and well, as a gift to whoever it serves. Then stop on time.
3.look: Chardin paints a kitchen maid who has stopped in the middle of her work. A knife and a vegetable rest in her lap, and her gaze has drifted off. It is the plainest of moments, peeling vegetables, yet Chardin gives it the same care, the same warm light and patient painting, that others gave to kings. That is the quiet argument of the picture. Ordinary work, done by ordinary people, is worth looking at, and worth doing well.
3.psalmNote: This verse ends the psalm credited to Moses, which spends most of its length on how short life is. Having faced that, it asks for one thing: that the work of our hands might last. For people who farmed and built by hand, this was a daily prayer. It gives meaning to the most ordinary task.
3.prayer: God of good work, establish the work of my hands today. Let the dull tasks matter, because they serve someone. Help me do one thing carefully and well, as a gift, and then help me rest, trusting that what lasts is in your hands. Amen.

3.title: Keeping Faith
3.line: Wednesday is for faithfulness: God's to us, and ours to God and to each other.
3.ideaLine: What do you hope to be like when you are old, and are you becoming it?

psalm.text: Yes, even when I am old and grey-haired, God, don't forsake me, until I have declared your strength to the next generation.

reading.text: Even to old age I am he, and even to grey hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear. Yes, I will carry, and will deliver.

midday.text: They will still produce fruit in old age. They will be full of sap and green.

evening.text: So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.

3.intention: Call or visit someone older than you today, and ask them what they have learned that they wish they had known sooner.
3.look: An older woman in a black dress, white ruff and lace cuffs sits upright in a wooden chair, turned slightly towards us. Hals had a reputation for quick, lively brushwork, and here he paints a face that has clearly lived sixty years and does not hide it. Her dignity comes not from looking young but from looking settled and steady in herself. It is a question worth asking in front of her: what kind of person is your life quietly shaping you into, and is it the person you hope to be?
3.psalmNote: This psalm is prayed by someone who has trusted God since childhood and now faces old age. The fear is being set aside, but the hope is bigger: to pass on what has been learned. Growing older here is not decline but a task, to tell the next generation what you have seen.
3.prayer: Lord, you have carried me from the beginning and promise to carry me to the end. As I grow older, make me kinder, wiser and more grateful, not more anxious. Give me something true to hand on, and teach me to listen to those who are older than me. Amen.

3.title: Keeping Faith
3.line: Wednesday is for faithfulness: God's to us, and ours to God and to each other.
3.ideaLine: If someone read your bank statement, what would they say you love?

psalm.text: If riches increase, don't set your heart on them.

reading.text: For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

midday.text: For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can't carry anything out.

evening.text: Better is a little that the righteous has, than the abundance of many wicked.

3.intention: Look at what you spent last week. Choose one thing to give up this week, and give that money to someone who needs it.
3.look: This small panel tells part of the life of Saint Anthony of Egypt. Inside a courtyard, a line of women, children and men waits before the haloed young Anthony. As a young man he heard in church Jesus’ words to sell what you have and give to the poor, and he did it, giving away his inheritance before going into the desert. The painter shows the gift in an ordinary, practical way: a queue of real people. Money becomes holy when it reaches someone.
3.psalmNote: Psalm 62 is about where we place our trust. The writer has learned that power and wealth cannot hold a person up, and only God can. Notice the psalm does not say riches are evil. It says not to set your heart on them. Our money follows our heart, and sometimes our heart can be moved by moving our money.
3.prayer: God, everything I have is a gift from you. Loosen my grip on what I own, and set my heart on what lasts. Show me one way to use my money today that would make someone’s life lighter, and give me the freedom to do it gladly. Amen.

4.title: Friends at the Table
4.line: Thursday remembers the Last Supper, when Jesus ate with his friends on the night before he died.
4.ideaLine: A welcome costs little and can change a life. Who could you make room for?

psalm.text: You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies. You anoint my head with oil. My cup runs over.

reading.text: But when you make a feast, ask the poor, the maimed, the lame, or the blind; and you will be blessed, because they don't have the resources to repay you.

midday.text: Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you, to the glory of God.

evening.text: Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him and will dine with him, and he with me.

4.intention: Invite someone who rarely gets asked: for coffee, a meal, or just a proper conversation.
4.look: Van Ostade shows a Dutch family outside their house, vines climbing the brick, with children playing, a dog and a chicken in the yard. We look down into an open, lived-in courtyard where the household happens in plain view. Nothing is closed off, and that openness is the heart of hospitality: not a perfect home, just a door left ajar and a life you are willing to share. Jesus said to invite those who can’t pay you back. A welcome like that costs little, and can change everything for someone.
4.psalmNote: Psalm 23 imagines God as a generous host who lays a table, pours oil on the guest’s head and fills the cup to overflowing. In the ancient Near East, welcoming a guest meant protecting them, even from their enemies. The psalm says God welcomes us like that. Having been welcomed, we can open our own doors.
4.prayer: Generous God, you set a table for me and fill my cup to overflowing. Open my door today, and my heart with it. Show me someone who rarely gets asked, and give me the courage to invite them, expecting nothing back. Amen.

4.title: Friends at the Table
4.line: Thursday remembers the Last Supper, when Jesus ate with his friends on the night before he died.
4.ideaLine: Something happens when people eat together. When did a shared meal last change your day?

psalm.text: Wine that makes the heart of man glad, oil to make his face to shine, and bread that strengthens man's heart.

reading.text: Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart.

midday.text: Go your way—eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart.

evening.text: When he had sat down at the table with them, he took the bread and gave thanks. Breaking it, he gave it to them. Their eyes were opened and they recognized him.

4.intention: Share one meal today with someone else, and before you begin, say thank you for the food and for them.
4.look: Vuillard paints a family meal in a garden: a man and woman at a table, a baby with them, vines climbing the walls all round. The whole scene is made of loose dabs and smudges, so the people seem to melt into the warm colour around them. That is how a good shared meal feels. Nobody is posed; the edges between people soften. Jesus chose a meal to leave his friends something to remember him by, and Christians have been breaking bread together ever since.
4.psalmNote: This psalm celebrates everything God made, from mountains to sea creatures, and here it pauses on the table: wine, oil and bread. These were the staples of daily life, and the psalmist sees them as gifts. Christians later found in bread and wine the meal Jesus gave his friends, the gladness of sharing one table.
4.prayer: Generous God, thank you for bread that strengthens and wine that makes the heart glad. Thank you for the people who have shared their table with me. Today, help me share mine, and to notice the gift in an ordinary meal eaten together. Amen.

4.title: Friends at the Table
4.line: Thursday remembers the Last Supper, when Jesus ate with his friends on the night before he died.
4.ideaLine: Everyone needs a place where they are missed when they are not there. Where is yours?

psalm.text: See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity.

reading.text: When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. When one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.

midday.text: God sets the lonely in families.

evening.text: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow.

4.intention: Turn up for something local today or this week: a club, a choir, a service, a neighbour's door.
4.look: John Singleton Copley painted his own family gathered on a sofa, children tumbling over their parents, the grandfather seated on the left and Copley himself standing at the back looking out at us. He made it soon after they had left Boston for London, a family reunited in a new country. Look at how close they sit, hands touching, children leaning on adults. Whatever else had changed, this was where they belonged. Everyone needs a place like this, where you are known, held and missed when you are gone.
4.psalmNote: This short psalm was sung by pilgrims travelling to Jerusalem, families and strangers walking together. It celebrates living side by side in harmony, comparing it to fragrant oil and refreshing dew. Belonging, it says, is not just pleasant; it is where God pours out blessing.
4.prayer: Lord, you made us for each other, not to be alone. Thank you for the places where I belong. Show me where I am missed and where I could turn up today. And help me to make room for someone who has nowhere to belong. Amen.

4.title: Friends at the Table
4.line: Thursday remembers the Last Supper, the meal Jesus shared with his friends the night before he died.
4.ideaLine: Do you have a friend who tells you the truth, and are you that friend to anyone?

psalm.text: Let the righteous strike me, it is kindness; let him reprove me, it is like oil on the head; don't let my head refuse it.

reading.text: The wounds of a friend are faithful, although the kisses of an enemy are profuse.

midday.text: A friend loves at all times; and a brother is born for adversity.

evening.text: Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend's countenance.

4.intention: Thank a friend who once told you something hard that you needed to hear.
4.look: Richard Norris Brooke paints a minister visiting a family at home. He sits by the table in his black coat, white-haired and bespectacled, his top hat and book set down, chin lifted as he talks. The family gathers round. Brooke shows a welcome that is warm but not flattering: the visitor is there to encourage, and sometimes to say what needs saying. Honest friends are like that. They come in, sit at the table, and tell you the truth because they care.
4.psalmNote: Psalm 141 has long been an evening prayer. The writer asks to be kept from bad company and smooth talk, and then says something surprising: a rebuke from a good person is a kindness, like oil poured on a guest’s head, the ancient sign of honour. Honest friendship is a gift we have to choose to receive.
4.prayer: God, thank you for the friends who tell me the truth. Soften me so I don’t bristle when correction comes from someone who loves me. And make me that kind of friend to others: honest, gentle and on their side. Amen.

5.title: The Cross
5.line: Every Friday remembers the day Jesus died on the cross, and the love that held nothing back.
5.ideaLine: Nobody gets through life alone. Whose load could you help carry today?

psalm.text: Cast your burden on the Lord and he will sustain you.

reading.text: Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.

midday.text: Surely he has borne our sickness and carried our suffering.

evening.text: Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears our burdens, even the God who is our salvation.

5.intention: Ask someone who is struggling what would actually help, and then do it.
5.look: About two dozen people are gathered around Jesus as he carries his cross through the countryside, in clothes of bright red and blue. Some follow, some watch, some turn away. The cross sits at the centre, and everyone in the picture has to decide how near they will come to it. The Gospels tell of one man, Simon of Cyrene, who was made to help carry it. Today asks whether we will be bystanders or helpers when someone near us is struggling under a weight.
5.psalmNote: Psalm 55 comes from someone betrayed by a close friend, longing to fly away from it all. In the middle of that pain comes this advice: throw your burden onto the Lord. It does not pretend the weight is light. It says we were never meant to carry it alone, and that God will hold us up.
5.prayer: Lord Jesus, you carried your cross for us, and you know how heavy life can be. I cast my burdens on you this morning. Show me someone who is struggling, give me the humility to ask what would really help, and the will to do it. Amen.

5.title: The Cross
5.line: Every Friday remembers the day Jesus died on the cross, and the love that held nothing back.
5.ideaLine: A grudge is heavy to carry. What would it take to set one down?

psalm.text: As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us.

reading.text: Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing.”

midday.text: Bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.

evening.text: But there is forgiveness with you, therefore you are feared.

5.intention: Name one grudge you are holding. Today, wish that person well, even if you cannot yet say it to them.
5.look: David was on his way to take revenge on a man named Nabal, who had insulted him. Nabal’s wife Abigail rode out to meet him with food for his men, knelt, and talked him out of it. Rubens paints the moment: Abigail kneeling, David reaching out his hand to her. A whole crowd has stopped to watch. A grudge that could have ended in bloodshed ends in a meeting instead. Sometimes one person’s courage is enough to let us set ours down.
5.psalmNote: This psalm sings of God’s mercy, and here it reaches for the widest picture it can find. East and west never meet; that is how far God puts our wrongs from us. It was prayed by people who knew they had failed. Being forgiven like that makes it easier, slowly, to forgive others.
5.prayer: Merciful God, you have taken my wrongs as far away as east is from west. I am still holding on to someone else’s. Loosen my grip. Even if I cannot yet forgive fully, help me wish them well today, and leave the rest with you. Amen.

5.title: The Cross
5.line: Every Friday remembers the day Jesus died on the cross, and the love that held nothing back.
5.ideaLine: Pain is part of every life. What do you need when it is your turn to hurt?

psalm.text: The Lord is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.

reading.text: We are pressed on every side, yet not crushed; perplexed, yet not to despair; pursued, yet not forsaken; struck down, yet not destroyed.

midday.text: Jesus wept.

evening.text: He heals the broken in heart, and binds up their wounds.

5.intention: Be gentle with your own hurt today, and sit for a while with someone else in theirs without trying to fix it.
5.look: Seven people crowd around the body of Jesus, their eyes red and tears running down their faces. Solario paints no explanations or speeches, only grief and nearness; nobody here can fix anything, but they can stay close, hold him and weep together. On a Friday, when Christians remember the cross, this painting says something important: pain is not shameful, and it is not meant to be borne alone. Sometimes the best thing we can offer is to stay.
5.psalmNote: This psalm comes from someone who has been through deep trouble and been rescued. It does not promise that the broken-hearted will avoid pain, but that God comes close to them. For people in grief that was the comfort: not an answer, but a presence.
5.prayer: Lord, you know what it is to suffer, and you stay near the broken-hearted. Be close to me in what hurts, and close to those I love who are struggling. Give me the patience to sit with someone today without rushing them to feel better. Amen.

5.title: The Cross
5.line: Every Friday remembers the day Jesus died on the cross, and the love that held nothing back.
5.ideaLine: What would you do today if you were a little less afraid?

psalm.text: The Lord is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear?

reading.text: Haven't I commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Don't be afraid. Don't be dismayed, for the Lord your God is with you wherever you go.

midday.text: Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all you who hope in the Lord.

evening.text: In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world.

5.intention: Do one right thing today that costs you something: speak up for someone, or own a mistake in front of others.
5.look: This small painting, not much bigger than a postcard, shows Saint George in armour on a rearing grey horse, pinning a winged dragon to the ground with his lance. Behind him the princess kneels, and a city and mountains stretch into the distance. Look at how ordinary that world is beyond the fight: roads, water, houses. Courage protects the everyday. Most of us will never face a dragon, but each day asks a little bravery for someone else’s sake.
5.psalmNote: Psalm 27 comes from someone facing real threats, enemies and armies. The writer does not deny the danger. He simply asks: if God is my light, whom shall I fear? Courage in the Bible is rarely the absence of fear. It is fear that has looked up and remembered it is not alone.
5.prayer: Lord, you are my light and my safety. I name before you what makes me afraid today. Give me just enough courage for the right thing in front of me, to speak up or to own my mistake, and remind me that you go with me wherever I go. Amen.

6.title: Rest and Remembering
6.line: Saturday is the day of rest and the quiet day after the cross, when the dead are remembered with hope.
6.ideaLine: We are told we always need more. What would it feel like to have enough?

psalm.text: The Lord is my shepherd; I shall lack nothing.

reading.text: Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it.

midday.text: Give me neither poverty nor riches. Feed me with the food that is needful for me.

evening.text: Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.

6.intention: Go a whole day without buying anything you don't need, and notice what you already have.
6.look: Chardin painted ordinary things with great love: a glass, a jug, peaches in a basket, other fruit laid along a ledge. Light falls from the upper left and the simple objects seem to glow. There is nothing rare or expensive here, yet the picture feels full. That is what enough looks like: not having everything, but seeing what is in front of you as a gift. Chardin invites us to pause before our own table and find it already rich.
6.psalmNote: Psalm 23 was probably written by someone who knew shepherding well. A good shepherd leads the flock to grass and water, so the sheep lack nothing they truly need. The psalm doesn’t promise everything we want. It says that, cared for by God, we have enough, and that contentment is possible even in hard places.
6.prayer: Shepherd God, you know what I need better than I do. Free me today from the itch for more. Help me to see what is already on my table as a gift, and to rest in your care, lacking nothing that truly matters. Amen.

6.title: Rest and Remembering
6.line: Saturday is the day of rest and the quiet day after the cross, when the dead are remembered with hope.
6.ideaLine: We stand on the shoulders of people we never met. Who carried something good down to you?

psalm.text: So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.

reading.text: Therefore let's also, seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let's run with perseverance the race that is set before us.

midday.text: One generation will commend your works to another, and will declare your mighty acts.

evening.text: In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you alone, Lord, make me live in safety.

6.intention: Remember someone who has died and shaped you. Tell someone else a story about them.
6.look: An old woman in black, with a wide white collar, sits with a book and looks away to our left, as if remembering something. The painting comes from Rembrandt and his workshop, and its light falls gently on her face and hands against a dark background. We don’t know her name. But she stands for all the people who carried faith, stories and wisdom down to us, often through quiet lives we never saw. Every one of us is someone’s inheritance.
6.psalmNote: This prayer is credited to Moses, and it sets our brief lives against God’s eternity. To count our days is not to be gloomy but to be wise, knowing life is a gift with an end. On Saturday it turns our thoughts to those whose days are done, and to what they handed on.
6.prayer: Eternal God, our days pass quickly, but they are not lost to you. Thank you for the people who came before me and handed on something good. Hold those I love who have died, and help me live so that I pass something good on too. Amen.

6.title: Rest and Remembering
6.line: Saturday is the day of rest and the quiet day after the cross, when the dead are remembered with hope.
6.ideaLine: Gratitude changes how a day feels. What have you been given that you have not yet thanked anyone for?

psalm.text: Praise the Lord, my soul, and don't forget all his benefits.

reading.text: In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.

midday.text: One of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, glorifying God with a loud voice. He fell on his face at Jesus' feet, giving him thanks.

evening.text: It is a good thing to give thanks to the Lord, to sing praises to your name, Most High, to proclaim your loving kindness in the morning, and your faithfulness every night.

6.intention: Write down three things from this week you are grateful for, and thank one person in writing.
6.look: In a dark room, the light falls on an older woman and a young boy. She has stopped work at the spinning wheel and sits with a loaf in her lap, about to cut it, while the boy stands before her saying grace. It is an ordinary household moment, but van Mieris makes it glow: before the bread is eaten, someone stops to say thank you. Gratitude does this to a day, turning what we take for granted back into a gift.
6.psalmNote: The writer talks to himself here, telling his own soul to remember. The people who first prayed this psalm knew how easy it is to forget God’s kindness once the crisis passes. Gratitude, for them, was a deliberate act of memory, and it still is.
6.prayer: Lord, my soul is quick to forget. Today I want to remember your kindness: the bread on my table, the people who love me, and the help I have not deserved. Give me grace to say thank you, to you and to someone who needs to hear it. Amen.

6.title: Rest and Remembering
6.line: Saturday is the old day of rest, and the day Christ lay in the tomb: a day to stop, give thanks and remember.
6.ideaLine: What would it be like to let go of tomorrow's worries for one afternoon?

psalm.text: How many are your works! In wisdom, you have made them all. The earth is full of your riches.

reading.text: See the birds of the sky, that they don't sow, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns. Your heavenly Father feeds them. Aren't you of much more value than they?

midday.text: The birds of the sky nest by them. They sing among the branches.

evening.text: In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you alone, Lord, make me live in safety.

6.intention: Write tomorrow’s biggest worry on a piece of paper, put it away, and give this afternoon to someone you love.
6.look: Martin Johnson Heade travelled to Brazil to paint hummingbirds, and here three of them gather round a tiny nest on a mossy branch, beside a pink and purple orchid. Behind them lies a hazy forest. The birds glitter like jewels. Nothing in the picture is planning or storing up; everything is simply alive and fed. Jesus pointed to the birds for this reason. If such small, bright creatures are cared for, perhaps we can put tomorrow’s worries down for an afternoon.
6.psalmNote: Psalm 104 is a hymn of wonder at creation. It names springs, cedars, storks in the fir trees, young lions, the wide sea, and sees God’s wisdom in all of it. Its first singers had no wildlife films, only their own eyes and a sense that the world was full to the brim. That wonder is the beginning of letting go of worry.
6.prayer: Creator God, the earth is full of your riches, and you feed even the smallest birds. I hand you tomorrow’s worries now. Let me rest today in your care, enjoy what is in front of me, and trust that I am worth more to you than I fear. Amen.

6.title: Rest and Remembering
6.line: Saturday is the old day of rest, and the day Christ lay in the tomb: a day to stop, give thanks and remember.
6.ideaLine: What would you notice about your own life if you stopped measuring it against other people's?

psalm.text: The lines have fallen to me in pleasant places. Yes, I have a good inheritance.

reading.text: Be free from the love of money, content with such things as you have.

midday.text: The life of the body is a heart at peace, but envy rots the bones.

evening.text: Return to your rest, my soul, for the Lord has dealt bountifully with you.

6.intention: Each time you catch yourself envying someone today, name one good thing in your own life instead. Tonight, write three of them down.
6.look: Mary Cassatt shows a young woman sitting on a green bench, her elbow hooked over the top slat and her head tilted to rest, lost in her own thoughts. The red zinnia in the title gives the picture a spot of colour. She is not looking at anyone else or trying to be seen, simply present to her own life. Cassatt, an American who worked among the Impressionists in Paris, often painted women in such private, unhurried moments. This is what it is like to stop comparing: to sit in your own place and find it good.
6.psalmNote: Psalm 16 uses the language of land. In ancient Israel, plots were marked out by measuring lines and handed down as an inheritance. The psalmist looks at their share and calls it pleasant and good. Not a bigger share than the neighbours’, just good. It is the voice of someone who has stopped looking over the fence.
6.prayer: Lord, the lines have fallen for me in pleasant places, though I often fail to notice. Free me today from measuring my life against other people’s. Show me what is good in my own share, and make me glad, not envious, when others are blessed. Amen.
